</PracticeLink>

m2/coordinate-geometry.title: Coordinate Geometry
m2/coordinate-geometry.content:
## MM3.1 Equations of straight lines

Start with the familiar $y=mx+c$ and get comfortable with what $m$ and $c$ actually mean, since almost everything else in this section builds on it.

$m$ is the **gradient**, and it's worth having several ways of thinking about it in your head at once, because different questions reward different pictures:

- **Steepness**: the bigger $|m|$, the steeper the line. Positive $m$ climbs left-to-right; negative $m$ falls left-to-right.
- **Rate of change**: $y$ changes $m$ times as fast as $x$ does. A gradient of $2$ means "every time $x$ goes up by $1$, $y$ goes up by $2$" — and this is the picture that carries over directly to tangents and differentiation later.
- **Angle**: $m=\tan\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle the line makes with the positive $x$-axis (assuming equal scales on both axes). A $45°$ line has gradient $\tan45°=1$, matching $y=x$; a $135°$ line has gradient $\tan135°=-1$, matching $y=-x$.

<FormulaCard title="Gradient between two points">
$$
m = \frac{y_1-y_2}{x_1-x_2}
$$

Keep the $x$'s and $y$'s in the same order top and bottom — swap one but not the other and you flip the sign of the gradient.
</FormulaCard>

Horizontal and vertical lines are the two special cases worth memorising outright rather than trying to force into $y=mx+c$: a horizontal line has gradient $0$ and equation $y=\text{some number}$; a vertical line has no gradient (people sometimes say "infinite gradient", which is a bit of a fudge) and equation $x=\text{some number}$. The $x$-axis itself is $y=0$ and the $y$-axis is $x=0$.

<Trap title="Vertical lines don't fit y = mx + c">
If a question's answer would require $x=\text{constant}$, don't try to shoehorn it into $y=mx+c$ — there's no finite $m$ that works. Spot vertical (and horizontal) lines as special cases before you start substituting.
</Trap>

### Parallel and perpendicular lines

<FormulaCard title="Parallel and perpendicular conditions">
Lines $y=m_1x+c_1$ and $y=m_2x+c_2$ are:

$$
\text{parallel} \iff m_1=m_2
$$

$$
\text{perpendicular} \iff m_1m_2=-1
$$
</FormulaCard>

Parallel lines have the same steepness, so it makes sense they share a gradient. The perpendicular condition is less obvious on sight, but you can convince yourself of it by rotating a line $90°$ and tracking what happens to its "along" and "up" steps — they swap and one flips sign. It's a genuinely useful exercise to sit down with a diagram of two perpendicular lines, drop the right-angled triangles under each, and show the similar-triangles argument for why $m_1m_2=-1$ yourself, rather than just banking the fact.

### Finding the equation of a line

You need exactly two pieces of information to pin down a line, and they come in two flavours.

**Case 1 — a point and a gradient.** If $(x_1,y_1)$ lies on a line of gradient $m$, then any other point $(x,y)$ on the line must give the same gradient when joined to $(x_1,y_1)$:

<FormulaCard title="Point-gradient form">
$$
\frac{y-y_1}{x-x_1}=m \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y-y_1=m(x-x_1)
$$
</FormulaCard>

Equally you can substitute $(x_1,y_1)$ straight into $y=mx+c$ and solve for $c$ — both routes get you to the same place, so use whichever feels quicker for the numbers in front of you.

<WorkedExample title="Point and gradient">
Find the equation of the line through $(3,2)$ with gradient $4$.

$$
y-2=4(x-3) \ \Longrightarrow\ y=4x-10
$$
</WorkedExample>

**Case 2 — two points.** Given $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$, work out the gradient first using the formula above, then drop it into the point-gradient form with either point.

<WorkedExample title="Two points">
Find the equation of the line through $(-2,5)$ and $(-4,-7)$.

$$
m=\frac{5-(-7)}{-2-(-4)}=\frac{12}{2}=6
$$

Using $(-2,5)$: $y-5=6(x+2) \Rightarrow y=6x+17$.
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Spot a shortcut when one point is the origin">
If one of your two points is $(0,0)$, the gradient is just $\dfrac{y}{x}$ of the other point, and the line is simply $y=mx$ — no need to set up simultaneous equations to find $c$, since it's obviously $0$.
</Shortcut>

<Trap title="Sign errors are the biggest risk in line questions">
Every step here involves subtracting coordinates, and it is very easy to lose a minus sign along the way — especially with negative coordinates. Slow down when substituting and double-check your answer by plugging both original points back into your final equation.
</Trap>

Finally, you'll see lines written either as $y=mx+c$ or as $ax+by+c=0$. Both are common and you should be able to move between them freely — just don't assume the $c$ in $ax+by+c=0$ is the $y$-intercept, because it isn't (it's an unfortunate clash of notation, not a deep fact).

## MM3.2 The equation of a circle

Picture a circle of radius $1$ centred at the origin. Every point $(x,y)$ on it is a distance $1$ from the origin, and Pythagoras turns that sentence directly into algebra:

$$
x^2+y^2=1
$$

Scaling the radius to $r$ and shifting the centre to $(a,b)$ (either by redoing Pythagoras or by treating it as a graph transformation) gives the general equation you should know cold:

<FormulaCard title="Equation of a circle, centre-radius form">
$$
(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2
$$

Centre $(a,b)$, radius $r$. Points inside satisfy $<$, points outside satisfy $>$.
</FormulaCard>

You should be able to read off the centre and radius of a circle on sight: $(x-2)^2+(y-3)^2=25$ has centre $(2,3)$ and radius $5$ — **not** $25$, since it's $r^2$ that equals $25$.

### The expanded form

Circles are also written as $x^2+y^2+ax+by+c=0$. To get back to centre-radius form, collect the $x$'s and $y$'s separately and complete the square on each.

<WorkedExample title="Completing the square to find centre and radius">
Find the centre and radius of $x^2+y^2+4x+2y-12=0$.

$$
(x^2+4x)+(y^2+2y)-12=0
$$

$$
(x+2)^2-4+(y+1)^2-1-12=0
$$

$$
(x+2)^2+(y+1)^2=17
$$

Centre $(-2,-1)$, radius $\sqrt{17}$.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Not every equation of this shape is a circle">
Try the same process on $x^2+y^2-4x-6y+20=0$ and you'll land on $(x-2)^2+(y-3)^2=-7$. A sum of squares can never be negative, so this equation has no real solutions at all — it isn't a circle. Whenever you complete the square, check the right-hand side comes out positive before declaring victory.
</Trap>

<Tip title="Divide through first if the coefficients of x² and y² aren't 1">
$2x^2+2y^2-4x-8y-19=0$ doesn't look like the standard form, but dividing everything by $2$ fixes that immediately: $x^2+y^2-2x-4y-\frac{19}{2}=0$. Then complete the square as usual.
</Tip>

### Lines meeting circles

A line can cross a circle twice, touch it once (tangent), or miss it completely. Substituting the line's equation into the circle's always produces a quadratic, so the number of intersections is controlled by the discriminant — this is the single idea underneath almost every "line meets circle" question.

<WorkedExample title="Finding a tangent condition">
Find the values of $c$ for which $y=2x+c$ is tangent to $(x-3)^2+(y-2)^2=9$.

Substitute and expand:

$$
(x-3)^2+(2x+c-2)^2=9 \ \Longrightarrow\ 5x^2+2(c-7)x+(c-2)^2=0
$$

Tangency means one repeated root, so the discriminant is zero:

$$
4(c-7)^2-20(c-2)^2=0 \ \Longrightarrow\ c-7=\pm\sqrt5\,(c-2)
$$

Solving each sign gives the two values of $c$ — there are two tangent lines with this gradient, one on each side of the circle, which is exactly what a quick sketch would lead you to expect.
</WorkedExample>

For "shortest distance between a line and a circle" questions, it's often cleanest to translate everything so the circle sits at the origin first (subtracting off the centre from every $x$ and $y$), since that strips out a lot of the arithmetic clutter and leaves a much simpler picture to reason about geometrically.

<Shortcut title="Distance from a line, then subtract the radius">
The shortest distance from a line to a circle is (distance from the centre to the line) minus the radius. You aren't expected to know the point-to-line distance formula for the TMUA/ESAT, but if you do use it, make sure you can derive it — don't just plug numbers into a memorised formula you don't understand.
</Shortcut>

## MM3.3 Circle theorems

These come up regularly, and because they're often taught early and then not revisited, they're an easy set of marks to lose to rustiness rather than difficulty. Make sure every one of the following is instantly available, not something you have to reconstruct in the exam:

<FormulaCard title="The circle theorems">

- The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
- The tangent at any point on a circle is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
- The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is twice the angle it subtends at the circumference.
- The angle in a semicircle is a right angle.
- Angles in the same segment are equal.
- Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to $180°$.
- The angle between a tangent and a chord at the point of contact equals the angle in the alternate segment.

</FormulaCard>

You don't need to be able to reproduce formal proofs of these from memory, but you should genuinely understand *why* each one is true — what's being assumed, which triangles or angles are doing the work — rather than treating them as facts to recall. It's also worth thinking about the converse of each theorem (e.g. "if the angle in a triangle inscribed in a circle is $90°$, the hypotenuse is a diameter"), since converses show up in proof-style questions.

A few habits make circle-theorem questions much more manageable:

1. **Angle chasing** — fill in every angle you can, hunting especially for isosceles triangles (two sides are radii) and right angles (anything in a semicircle).
2. **Rotating your mental picture of the diagram** — sometimes a relationship is only obvious once you stop looking at the diagram in the orientation it was drawn in.
3. **Adding your own lines** — a well-chosen extra radius, chord, or diameter often turns an opaque diagram into an obvious one.
4. **Thinking dynamically** — imagine sliding a point around the circle and ask which angles stay fixed and which change; this builds intuition for why theorems like "angles in the same segment are equal" have to be true.

<Tip title="Play with an interactive circle-theorem tool">
If circle theorems feel rusty, spend ten minutes with any interactive geometry site that lets you drag points around a circle and watch the angles update live — seeing the invariants hold as you move things is far more convincing (and memorable) than reading a static diagram.
</Tip>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- Gradient between two points: $m=\dfrac{y_1-y_2}{x_1-x_2}$. Gradient also equals $\tan\theta$ with the positive $x$-axis (equal scales).
- Point-gradient form: $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$. Vertical lines are $x=\text{constant}$; horizontal lines are $y=\text{constant}$.
- Parallel: $m_1=m_2$. Perpendicular: $m_1m_2=-1$.
- Circle, centre-radius form: $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2$, centre $(a,b)$, radius $r$.
- To find centre/radius from $x^2+y^2+ax+by+c=0$: complete the square on the $x$'s and $y$'s separately. Check the right-hand side is positive.
- Line meets circle: substitute to get a quadratic, then use the discriminant — two real roots (crosses twice), zero (tangent), negative (misses).
- Circle theorems: perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre; tangent ⟂ radius; angle at centre = twice angle at circumference; angle in a semicircle = $90°$; angles in the same segment are equal; opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to $180°$; tangent-chord angle = angle in the alternate segment.

m2/differentiation.title: Differentiation
m2/differentiation.content:
## MM6.1 The derivative as a gradient and a rate of change

The **derivative** of $f(x)$ at a point is the gradient of the tangent to $y=f(x)$ there — how much $y$ changes per unit change in $x$. Gradient is just a rate of change: the gradient of a distance–time graph is speed, and the gradient of a speed–time graph is acceleration.

<FormulaCard title="Notation">
$$
\frac{dy}{dx}, \qquad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}, \qquad f'(x), \qquad f''(x)
$$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ (or $f'(x)$) is the **first derivative** — gradient of the tangent. $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ (or $f''(x)$) is the **second derivative** — the derivative of the derivative, i.e. how the gradient itself is changing.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Two different jobs, same expression">
$y=\ldots$ gives you a $y$-value for a given $x$-value. $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\ldots$ gives you the *gradient* at that $x$-value. Keep straight which question you're actually being asked — "find the value" versus "find the gradient" call for different expressions.
</Tip>

## MM6.2 Differentiating powers of x

<FormulaCard title="Power rule">
$$
\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(x^n\bigr) = nx^{n-1} \qquad \text{for any rational } n
$$

Differentiate term by term: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and constants differentiate to $0$.
</FormulaCard>

The TMUA/ESAT tests only sums of powers of $x$ (including fractional and negative powers) — no chain rule, product rule, or trig differentiation. If an expression isn't already in that form, **simplify first**.

<WorkedExample title="Simplify before differentiating">
Differentiate $y=\dfrac{(3x+2)^2}{\sqrt x}$.

Expand the numerator and split the fraction into separate powers of $x$:

$$
y = \frac{9x^2+12x+4}{x^{1/2}} = 9x^{3/2}+12x^{1/2}+4x^{-1/2}
$$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{27}{2}x^{1/2} + 6x^{-1/2} - 2x^{-3/2}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Term-by-term differentiation">
$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^3+7x^2-3x+11) = 3x^2+14x-3$ — differentiate each term independently ($n x^{n-1}$) and drop any constant term entirely; there's no need to think of the expression as a single object.
</Shortcut>

## MM6.3 Tangents, normals, stationary points, and monotonicity

<FormulaCard title="Tangent and normal at a point">
At $x=a$, the tangent has gradient $f'(a)$ and the normal (perpendicular to the tangent) has gradient $-\dfrac{1}{f'(a)}$. Both pass through $(a,f(a))$, so:

$$
y - f(a) = f'(a)(x-a) \qquad \text{(tangent)}, \qquad y - f(a) = -\frac{1}{f'(a)}(x-a) \qquad \text{(normal)}
$$
</FormulaCard>

**Stationary points** occur where $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$ — the tangent is horizontal. To classify a stationary point at $x=a$, use the second derivative:

<FormulaCard title="Classifying stationary points">
$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=0 \text{ and } \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0 \ \Rightarrow\ \text{minimum}, \qquad \frac{dy}{dx}=0 \text{ and } \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0 \ \Rightarrow\ \text{maximum}
$$
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Finding and classifying stationary points">
Find and classify the stationary points of $y=2x^3-3x^2-12x+6$.

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=6x^2-6x-12=6(x-2)(x+1)=0 \ \Rightarrow\ x=2 \text{ or } x=-1
$$

$$
\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12x-6
$$

At $x=-1$: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=-18<0$, so a **maximum**. At $x=2$: $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=18>0$, so a **minimum**. This also matches the shape of a positive cubic — maximum before minimum.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="dy/dx = 0 and d²y/dx² = 0 is inconclusive">
The second-derivative test is **sufficient but not necessary**. At a stationary point, $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}>0$ guarantees a minimum and $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}<0$ guarantees a maximum — but $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ tells you nothing on its own. $y=x^4$ has a minimum at $x=0$ with $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ there; $y=-x^4$ has a maximum at $x=0$ with $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$ there too. If the second derivative vanishes, check the sign of $\frac{dy}{dx}$ either side of the point instead.
</Trap>

<FormulaCard title="Strictly increasing and strictly decreasing">
$$
f'(x)>0 \text{ on } a<x<b \ \Rightarrow\ f \text{ strictly increasing on } a<x<b
$$

$$
f'(x)<0 \text{ on } a<x<b \ \Rightarrow\ f \text{ strictly decreasing on } a<x<b
$$
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="These conditions are sufficient, not necessary">
$f'(x)>0$ everywhere guarantees $f$ is strictly increasing — but a function can be strictly increasing without $f'(x)>0$ at *every* point (e.g. $y=x^3$ is strictly increasing through $x=0$, yet $f'(0)=0$). Don't try to run the implication backwards.
</Trap>

<Tip title="Points of inflexion: qualitative only">
Points of inflexion (e.g. the flat-through point of $y=x^3$ at the origin) are not formally examined, but you should recognise where they can appear when sketching simple polynomials — typically where a stationary point "flattens through" rather than turning into a clean max or min.
</Tip>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^n)=nx^{n-1}$ for any rational $n$; differentiate sums term by term, constants vanish.
- Simplify an expression into a sum of powers of $x$ *before* differentiating — no chain or product rule is tested.
- Tangent at $x=a$: gradient $f'(a)$. Normal at $x=a$: gradient $-\dfrac{1}{f'(a)}$.
- Stationary points: solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$. Classify with $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$: positive $\Rightarrow$ min, negative $\Rightarrow$ max, zero $\Rightarrow$ inconclusive (check either side instead).
- $f'(x)>0$ on an interval $\Rightarrow$ strictly increasing there; $f'(x)<0$ $\Rightarrow$ strictly decreasing — sufficient conditions, not necessary ones.

m2/exponentials-and-logarithms.title: Exponentials and Logarithms
m2/exponentials-and-logarithms.content:
## MM5.1 The graph of $y=a^x$

$y=a^x$ (for $a>0$) is worth sketching mentally in three cases, and you should be able to explain the features of each rather than just recognise the shapes:

- **$a>1$**: the classic growth curve. Always positive, passes through $(0,1)$, increases faster and faster as $x$ grows, and creeps towards $0$ (never reaching it) as $x\to-\infty$. The bigger $a$ is, the steeper the climb.
- **$a=1$**: $1^x=1$ for every $x$, so this is just the flat line $y=1$ — not really "exponential" behaviour at all, which is exactly why it's excluded as a base for logarithms later.
- **$0<a<1$**: a mirror image of the $a>1$ case — it's the same curve reflected in the $y$-axis, since $a^x=\left(\frac1a\right)^{-x}$ and $\frac1a>1$. It starts high, decreases, and creeps towards $0$ as $x\to+\infty$.

<Tip title="Play with a graphing tool">
Sketching these by hand is useful practice, but it's worth also plugging $y=2^x$, $y=10^x$ and a couple of fractional bases into a graphing package to see how quickly they grow and how the three cases above relate to each other.
</Tip>

Every curve $y=a^x$ (for $a\ne1$) passes through $(0,1)$, since $a^0=1$ regardless of $a$, and is never zero or negative — this is why the *domain* of the inverse function (the logarithm) will turn out to be restricted to positive numbers.

We don't consider $a<0$ here for the same reason this was excluded when you met indices with fractional powers: something like $(-4)^{\frac12}$ isn't a real number, so $a^x$ isn't even always defined once $a$ is negative.

## MM5.2 Laws of logarithms

A logarithm just answers the question "what power do I need?" — it's the inverse operation to raising a number to a power.

<FormulaCard title="The defining relationship">
$$
a^b=c \iff b=\log_a c
$$

Read $\log_a c$ as "the power $a$ must be raised to, to get $c$".
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Getting a feel for logs">
$$
\log_{10}100=2 \quad\text{because}\quad 10^2=100
$$

$$
\log_2 32=5 \quad\text{because}\quad 2^5=32
$$

$$
\log_2\tfrac12=-1 \quad\text{because}\quad 2^{-1}=\tfrac12
$$
</WorkedExample>

There are three conditions built into that definition that are easy to forget under exam pressure but genuinely matter:

<FormulaCard title="Conditions on the base and the argument">

- The base must be positive and not equal to $1$: $a>0,\ a\ne1$.
- You can only take the log of a positive number: $c>0$.
- The **result** of a log can be any real number, including negative or zero — there's no restriction on $b$.

</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="log of a non-positive number is undefined">
It's tempting to treat $\log_a c$ like an ordinary function that's defined everywhere, but $c\le0$ simply isn't in its domain — there's no real power you can raise a positive base to and get zero or a negative number. This has genuinely shown up as the crux of a past TMUA/ESAT question, so don't wave it away as a technicality.
</Trap>

### The log graph as a reflection

Since $\log_a x$ is the *inverse* of $a^x$, its graph is just $y=a^x$ reflected in the line $y=x$ — equivalently, swap the roles of the axes. Sketching $y=2^x$ and reading it "backwards" (start on the $y$-axis, trace across to the curve, then down to the $x$-axis) is exactly the process of taking a log base $2$.

<WorkedExample title="Reading off features of y = log_a x">
The graph of $y=\log_2 x$ is only defined for $x>0$ (matching the "$c>0$" condition above), and it crosses the $x$-axis at $x=1$ — because $\log_2 1=0$, since $2^0=1$.
</WorkedExample>

### The three log laws

Each of the following is really the "logarithm translation" of a familiar index law, and it's worth being able to derive each one rather than just quoting it — the trick each time is to raise $a$ to the power of both sides and use $a^{\log_a x}=x$ (which is just the definition of a logarithm restated).

<FormulaCard title="Addition, subtraction, and multiplication laws">
$$
\log_a x+\log_a y=\log_a(xy)
$$

$$
\log_a x-\log_a y=\log_a\left(\frac xy\right)
$$

$$
k\log_a x=\log_a\left(x^k\right)
$$
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Deriving the addition law">
Why does $\log_a x+\log_a y=\log_a(xy)$? Raise $a$ to the power of the left-hand side and use the index law $a^pa^q=a^{p+q}$:

$$
a^{\log_a x+\log_a y}=a^{\log_a x}\times a^{\log_a y}=x\times y
$$

So $a$ raised to $(\log_a x+\log_a y)$ gives $xy$ — which is exactly what "$\log_a x+\log_a y=\log_a(xy)$" means.
</WorkedExample>

There are two special cases worth knowing outright rather than re-deriving each time:

<FormulaCard title="Special cases">
$$
\log_a\frac1x=-\log_a x, \qquad \log_a a=1
$$
</FormulaCard>

$\log_a a=1$ should feel obvious once you see it — it's just asking "what power does $a$ need to be raised to, to get $a$?", and the answer is $1$.

<Shortcut title="Change of base — useful, but not examined">
The specification says you won't be asked a question that depends on the change-of-base formula, so don't spend exam time on it. It's still worth having in your back pocket as general mathematical knowledge, and it derives the same way as the laws above: let $p=\log_a b$, so $a^p=b$, then take $\log_c$ of both sides to get $p\log_c a=\log_c b$, giving

$$
\log_a b=\frac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}
$$

Setting $c=b$ gives the neat corollary $\log_a b=\dfrac{1}{\log_b a}$.
</Shortcut>

## MM5.3 Solving exponential equations

The core move for solving $a^x=b$ is to take logs of both sides — the base you choose is up to you, and a well-chosen base can make the algebra much cleaner.

<WorkedExample title="Choosing a convenient base">
Solve $5^{2x}=27$ exactly (i.e. leave the answer as a log expression, not a rounded decimal — many log values are irrational, just like surds, so rounding early throws away precision).

**Taking $\log_5$ of both sides:**

$$
\log_5 5^{2x}=\log_5 27=\log_5 3^3 \ \Longrightarrow\ 2x=3\log_5 3 \ \Longrightarrow\ x=\frac32\log_5 3
$$

**Taking $\log_3$ of both sides instead** (since $27=3^3$ is a clean power of $3$):

$$
\log_3 5^{2x}=\log_3 27 \ \Longrightarrow\ 2x\log_3 5=3 \ \Longrightarrow\ x=\frac{3}{2\log_3 5}
$$

Both are correct — they're the same number written two different ways, which you can check using the change-of-base identity above.
</WorkedExample>

<Tip title="Spot when the numbers on both sides share a common base">
Before reaching for logs, check whether both sides can be written as powers of the same number — $27=3^3$, $32=2^5$, and so on. If they can, you can often equate exponents directly without logs at all. Logs are the general-purpose tool; spotting a shared base is the shortcut.
</Tip>

Some equations aren't immediately in the form $a^x=b$ but can be reduced to it with a bit of algebraic manipulation first — commonly, spotting a hidden quadratic.

<WorkedExample title="Reducing to a hidden quadratic">
Solve $25^x-3\times5^x+2=0$.

Notice $25^x=(5^x)^2$, so substituting $u=5^x$ turns this into an ordinary quadratic:

$$
u^2-3u+2=0 \ \Longrightarrow\ (u-1)(u-2)=0 \ \Longrightarrow\ u=1 \text{ or } u=2
$$

Now undo the substitution: $5^x=1$ gives $x=0$ directly (since $5^0=1$), and $5^x=2$ gives $x=\log_5 2$.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Don't forget to undo the substitution">
Once you've solved for $u$, the question asked for $x$, not $u$ — it's an easy mark to drop by stopping one step too early after a substitution trick like $u=5^x$.
</Trap>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- $y=a^x$: passes through $(0,1)$, always positive. Growth curve for $a>1$, flat line $y=1$ for $a=1$, decay curve for $0<a<1$ (a reflection of the $a>1$ case in the $y$-axis).
- Definition: $a^b=c \iff b=\log_a c$, requiring $a>0,\ a\ne1,\ c>0$; $b$ itself can be any real number.
- $y=\log_a x$ is $y=a^x$ reflected in $y=x$; defined only for $x>0$, crosses the $x$-axis at $x=1$.
- $\log_a x+\log_a y=\log_a(xy)$; $\log_a x-\log_a y=\log_a\left(\frac xy\right)$; $k\log_a x=\log_a(x^k)$.
- Special cases: $\log_a\frac1x=-\log_a x$; $\log_a a=1$.
- Change of base (not examined, but useful): $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}$, giving $\log_a b=\dfrac1{\log_b a}$.
- To solve $a^x=b$: take logs of a well-chosen base, or spot a shared base and equate exponents directly. Watch for hidden quadratics via a substitution like $u=a^x$.

</PracticeLink>

m2/graphs-of-functions.title: Graphs of Functions
m2/graphs-of-functions.content:
Much of this topic is really a synthesis of things covered elsewhere in the specification — quadratics, trig, exponentials, logs, and differentiation all show up here as graphs rather than algebra. This guide focuses on the parts that are genuinely new: sketching a wide range of standard shapes on sight, the modulus function graphically, and the transformation rules that catch almost everyone out at least once.

## MM8.1 Recognising and sketching common graphs

You should be able to sketch, from the equation alone and without a calculator, the general shape of: lines, quadratics, cubics, trig functions, logs, exponentials, square roots, and — as a bonus — quartics and quintics.

<Tip title="Higher-power polynomials are worth exploring with a graphing package">
Spend time in Desmos plotting quadratics, cubics, quartics and quintics with different signs and numbers of roots. Pay particular attention to what the sign of the *leading* coefficient (the $x^2$ term in a quadratic, $x^3$ in a cubic, $x^4$ in a quartic, and so on) does to the ends of the graph, and how many times the curve can wiggle up and down in between.
</Tip>

The pattern worth internalising: a positive leading coefficient means the graph eventually goes up on both ends for even powers (quadratics, quartics), or up on the right and down on the left for odd powers (cubics, quintics) — and a negative leading coefficient flips all of that. The number of times the curve can turn is capped by its degree, but not every polynomial of a given degree uses up all its turns (e.g. $y=x^3$ has no turning points at all, even though a cubic *can* have two).

### The modulus function, graphically

You already know $|x|$ algebraically — it takes the positive value of whatever's inside. Graphically, the rule for sketching $y=|f(x)|$ from $y=f(x)$ is just that idea drawn out:

<Shortcut title="Sketch y = |f(x)| by flipping the negative part upward">
Sketch $y=f(x)$ as normal. Then reflect anything that sits *below* the $x$-axis up into the positive region (in the $x$-axis), and leave anything already above the axis untouched. This works because $|f(x)|$ only changes something when $f(x)$ is negative — that's exactly when it needs "flipping" to become positive.
</Shortcut>

<WorkedExample title="Modulus of a quadratic and of a line">
$y=(x+1)(x-2)$ is a $\cup$-shaped parabola dipping below the axis between $x=-1$ and $x=2$. For $y=|(x+1)(x-2)|$, that dip gets reflected upward, leaving a "W-ish" shape that touches the axis at $x=-1$ and $x=2$ and is never negative.

$y=x-2$ is a straight line crossing the axis at $x=2$, negative to the left of that and positive to the right. $y=|x-2|$ keeps the positive part unchanged and reflects the negative part, giving a V-shape with its vertex sitting on the axis at $x=2$.
</WorkedExample>

It's worth being able to write down the equation of each piece of a modulus graph once it's been sketched: the reflected (flipped) piece has equation $y=-f(x)$, and the untouched piece keeps $y=f(x)$.

<WorkedExample title="Solving an inequality by sketching">
Solve $x+4<|2x-1|$.

Sketch $y=x+4$ and $y=|2x-1|$ on the same axes and find where they cross. Since the modulus graph has two pieces, check both:

$$
x+4=2x-1 \implies x=5 \qquad\text{(where } 2x-1\text{ is the unflipped piece)}
$$

$$
x+4=-(2x-1) \implies x=-1 \qquad\text{(where the piece is flipped)}
$$

The inequality asks where the line sits *below* the modulus graph. Reading that off the sketch:

$$
x<-1 \ \text{ or } \ x>5
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Solving modulus inequalities purely algebraically loses the picture">
It's possible to solve modulus equations and inequalities with squaring or case-splitting, but for anything beyond the simplest cases a quick sketch tells you immediately how many crossing points to expect and which region satisfies the inequality — skipping the sketch is the most common way to lose track of a solution branch.
</Trap>

## MM8.2 Transformations of y = f(x)

This is the section that trips people up most, mainly because two of the four transformations do the *opposite* of what your gut expects. The fix is to always go back to what the notation actually means, rather than trying to memorise the rules as arbitrary facts.

The key idea throughout: $y=f(x)$ means "the $y$ value directly above a given $x$ is worked out using $f(x)$". Every transformation below is just a consequence of applying that same reading to a new expression.

<FormulaCard title="The four transformations">

| Transformation | Effect on $y=f(x)$ |
|---|---|
| $y=af(x)$ | vertical stretch, factor $a$, away from the $x$-axis (reflects in the $x$-axis too if $a<0$) |
| $y=f(x)+a$ | translation by $\begin{pmatrix}0\\a\end{pmatrix}$ |
| $y=f(x+a)$ | translation by $\begin{pmatrix}-a\\0\end{pmatrix}$ |
| $y=f(ax)$ | horizontal squash, factor $a$, towards the $y$-axis (reflects in the $y$-axis too if $a<0$) |

</FormulaCard>

**$y=af(x)$** is the intuitive one: every $y$ value gets multiplied by $a$, so the graph is stretched vertically away from the $x$-axis by a factor of $a$. If $0<a<1$ the graph gets "squashed" flatter rather than taller, and a negative $a$ additionally flips it upside down.

**$y=f(x)+a$** just adds $a$ to every $y$ value, so it's a straight vertical shift — up by $a$ if $a>0$, down if $a$ is negative.

**$y=f(x+a)$ is the counter-intuitive one.** It looks like adding something to $x$ should shift the graph right, but it actually shifts it *left* (for positive $a$).

<WorkedExample title="Why f(x + a) shifts the graph left, not right">
Take $f(x)=2^x$ and compare it with $f(x+3)$.

On $y=f(x)$: at $x=2$, $y=f(2)=4$; at $x=5$, $y=f(5)=32$.

On $y=f(x+3)$: at $x=2$, $y=f(2+3)=f(5)=32$; at $x=5$, $y=f(5+3)=f(8)=256$.

So the $y$ value sitting above $x=2$ on the new graph is the value that used to sit above $x=5$ on the old one — the "$32$" has moved three units to the **left**. In general, the graph of $y=f(x+a)$ is $y=f(x)$ translated by $\begin{pmatrix}-a\\0\end{pmatrix}$: left by $a$ when $a$ is positive, right by $a$ when $a$ is negative.
</WorkedExample>

**$y=f(ax)$** works the same way, and is similarly backwards from first instinct: it *squashes* the graph horizontally towards the $y$-axis by a factor of $a$, rather than stretching it.

<WorkedExample title="Why f(ax) squashes the graph">
Take $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+2$ and compare it with $f(2x)$.

At $x=1$ on $y=f(x)$: $y=f(1)=0$. On $y=f(2x)$, the $y$ value above $x=1$ is $f(2\times1)=f(2)=-2$ — which is the value that used to sit above $x=2$ on the original graph. The whole graph has been pulled in towards the $y$-axis by a factor of $2$.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="f(ax) means every x in the expression gets replaced by ax, not just multiplied outside">
Given $f(x)=x^2$, we have $f(3x)=(3x)^2=9x^2$ — **not** $3x^2$. The substitution replaces every occurrence of $x$, so any power or coefficient already attached to $x$ inside the function gets carried through the multiplication too. The same care applies to $f(x+a)$: given $f(x)=\cos(2x)$, $f\left(x-\frac\pi2\right)=\cos\left(2\left(x-\frac\pi2\right)\right)=\cos(2x-\pi)$, not $\cos(2x)-\frac\pi2$.
</Trap>

### Combining transformations — order matters

When you chain two transformations together, the order you apply them in changes the result, and it's easy to get it backwards.

<WorkedExample title="Getting the order right for cos(2x + π/6)">
Sketch $y=\cos x$ and use it to get to $y=\cos\left(2x+\frac\pi6\right)$.

**Squash by 2, then shift by $-\frac\pi6$ (wrong):**

$$
\cos x \to \cos 2x \to \cos\, 2\!\left(x+\frac\pi6\right)=\cos\left(2x+\frac\pi3\right) \quad\text{— not what we wanted}
$$

**Shift by $-\frac\pi6$, then squash by 2 (correct):**

$$
\cos x \to \cos\left(x+\frac\pi6\right) \to \cos\left(2x+\frac\pi6\right) \quad\checkmark
$$

The squash-then-shift order goes wrong because once $x$ has already been replaced by $2x$, a later "shift" of $\frac\pi6$ gets multiplied by that same $2$ before it lands. Equivalently, you could squash first and then shift by $-\frac{\pi}{12}$ instead of $-\frac\pi6$ — the amount of shift needed changes depending on when you apply it.
</WorkedExample>

<Tip title="When combining transformations, do the horizontal ones (shift, squash) in the order the algebra was built">
If a target expression looks like $f(ax+b)$, it was built as "replace $x$ by $x+\frac ba$, then squash by $a$" — factor the expression that way first (write $ax+b=a\left(x+\frac ba\right)$) and the correct order of transformations falls straight out, rather than needing to be guessed and checked.
</Tip>

### Composite functions f(g(x))

$f(g(x))$ — read "$f$ of $g$ of $x$" — means: take $g(x)$ and feed it in as the input to $f$. Since the $x$ in $f(x)$ is just a label for "whatever gets put in", you can substitute any expression in its place, including another function.

<WorkedExample title="Building f(g(x))">
Let $g(x)=2x$ and $f(x)=x^2+3x-2$.

Replace every $x$ in $f(x)$ with $g(x)$, then simplify:

$$
f(g(x)) = (2x)^2+3(2x)-2 = 4x^2+6x-2
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="f(g(x)) is generally not the same as g(f(x))">
Composition doesn't commute in general — swapping the order of $f$ and $g$ usually gives a different function entirely. Always apply the *inner* function first (the one closest to $x$), and don't assume you can reorder them.
</Trap>

## MM8.3 How m and c affect y = mx + c

You already know $m$ is the gradient and $c$ is the $y$-intercept, but it's worth seeing this as a composition of the transformations above, starting from $y=x$:

$$
y=x \ \to\ y=mx \ \to\ y=m\left(x+\frac cm\right)=mx+c
$$

or equivalently, shifting before stretching:

$$
y=x \ \to\ y=x+c \ \to\ y=mx+c
$$

Both routes land on the same graph, which is a good sanity check that the transformation rules are self-consistent — try following either sequence through with specific numbers for $m$ and $c$ to see it directly.

## MM8.4 How $a$, $b$, $c$ affect $y=a(x+b)^2+c$

The same idea applies to a quadratic written in completed-square form. One way to build it up (for $a>0$):

$$
y=x^2 \ \to\ y=(\sqrt a\,x)^2=ax^2 \ \to\ y=a(x+b)^2 \ \to\ y=a(x+b)^2+c
$$

using a horizontal squash by $\sqrt a$ to get the vertical stretch. Or, more directly, stretch vertically first:

$$
y=x^2 \ \to\ y=ax^2 \ \to\ y=a(x+b)^2 \ \to\ y=a(x+b)^2+c
$$

<Trap title="√a only works when a is positive">
The horizontal-squash route needs $\sqrt a$, which breaks down the moment $a$ is negative. When $a<0$, it's much simpler to just use the vertical-stretch route ($y=ax^2$ directly) rather than trying to force a square root through a negative number.
</Trap>

Either way, $b$ shifts the graph horizontally by $-b$ (left if $b>0$, following the same "backwards" rule as $f(x+a)$ above), and $c$ shifts it vertically by $c$ — matching exactly what you already know about the turning point of a quadratic sitting at $(-b,c)$.

## MM8.5–8.7 Already covered elsewhere

The remaining parts of this section aren't new content so much as graphical applications of ideas from other topics:

- **Using differentiation to sketch a graph** — finding stationary points and determining where a function increases or decreases — is covered in the differentiation guide.
- **Where a graph crosses the axes, and how many real roots a polynomial can have** is an application of the algebra and functions guide (factorising, the factor theorem, and the discriminant).
- **Reading simultaneous equations off intersecting graphs**: wherever two graphs cross, the coordinates of that point satisfy both equations simultaneously — solving a system algebraically and finding where two curves meet are exactly the same question asked two different ways.

## Formula and shortcut summary

- Leading coefficient of a polynomial controls end behaviour: positive means "up" on the right (and up on the left for even degree, down for odd); negative flips it.
- $y=|f(x)|$: sketch $y=f(x)$, then reflect anything below the $x$-axis upward, leaving the rest unchanged.
- $y=af(x)$: vertical stretch by $a$ (flips in the $x$-axis if $a<0$).
- $y=f(x)+a$: translation $\begin{pmatrix}0\\a\end{pmatrix}$.
- $y=f(x+a)$: translation $\begin{pmatrix}-a\\0\end{pmatrix}$ — shifts **left** for positive $a$, opposite to first instinct.
- $y=f(ax)$: horizontal squash by $a$ towards the $y$-axis (flips in the $y$-axis if $a<0$) — squashes, doesn't stretch.
- When combining a shift and a squash, factor the expression as $f(a(x+b/a))$ first to get the order right; shift-then-squash and squash-then-shift generally give different results.
- $f(g(x))$: substitute $g(x)$ for every $x$ in $f(x)$. Apply the inner function first; $f(g(x))\ne g(f(x))$ in general.

m2/integration.title: Integration
m2/integration.content:
## MM7.2 Integrating powers of x

Integration is the reverse of differentiation: $\int f(x)\,dx$ asks "what must have been differentiated to get $f(x)$?"

<FormulaCard title="Power rule for integration">
$$
\int kx^n\,dx = \frac{kx^{n+1}}{n+1}+c \qquad (n\ne-1)
$$

Only sums of powers of $x$ are tested (no substitution, parts, or $n=-1$). Simplify an expression into that form before integrating, and integrate term by term.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Don't forget +c for an indefinite integral">
Differentiating any constant gives $0$, so integrating "undoes" the derivative only up to an unknown constant — always append $+c$ unless you're doing a *definite* integral (with limits), where the constants cancel.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Simplify before integrating">
$$
\int(x-2)^2\,dx = \int x^2-4x+4\,dx = \frac{x^3}{3}-2x^2+4x+c
$$
</WorkedExample>

## MM7.1 Definite integration and the area between a curve and an axis

<FormulaCard title="Definite integral">
$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \Bigl[F(x)\Bigr]_a^b = F(b)-F(a), \qquad \text{where } F'(x)=f(x)
$$
</FormulaCard>

A definite integral is the sum of the (positive) areas **above** the $x$-axis minus the (positive) areas **below** it — not the same thing as "total area enclosed."

<Trap title="Definite integral ≠ area, when the curve crosses the axis">
$\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{3}x^5\,dx=0$ even though the curve clearly encloses nonzero area on each side of $x=0$ — the regions above and below the axis cancel. If a question asks for **area** (not "the value of the integral"), split the interval at every root of $f(x)$ inside it, integrate each piece separately, and add the *absolute values*.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Area vs. the raw definite integral">
Find the area between the $x$-axis, $x=0$, $x=2$, and $y=x^2-1$.

The curve crosses the axis at $x=1$, so split there:

$$
\int_0^1 x^2-1\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_0^1 = \frac13-1=-\frac23, \qquad \int_1^2 x^2-1\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_1^2 = \frac83-2-\left(\frac13-1\right)=\frac43
$$

Area $=\left|-\frac23\right|+\frac43=2$. (Contrast this with the raw integral $\int_0^2 x^2-1\,dx=\frac23$, which is a different, smaller number.)
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Symmetry can kill an integral without any calculation">
If $f(x)$ is **antisymmetric** about the $y$-axis (odd function, $f(-x)=-f(x)$), then $\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx=0$ — the negative-$x$ region exactly cancels the positive-$x$ region. This is why $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx=0$ and $\int_{-10}^{10}x^3\,dx=0$ instantly, with no working needed. If $f(x)$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis (even function), $\int_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,dx=2\int_0^a f(x)\,dx$ instead.
</Shortcut>

## MM7.3 The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

<FormulaCard title="Fundamental Theorem of Calculus">
$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b)-F(a), \quad \text{where } F'(x)=f(x), \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt = f(x)
$$

Swapping the limits flips the sign: $\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = -\int_b^a f(x)\,dx$.
</FormulaCard>

Integration and differentiation are inverse operations — this is why the two statements above hold, and why solving $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)$ for $y$ is just integrating $f(x)$.

## MM7.4 Combining integrals over equal or contiguous ranges

<FormulaCard title="Combining rules">
$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx+\int_a^b g(x)\,dx=\int_a^b\bigl[f(x)+g(x)\bigr]\,dx
$$

$$
\int_a^c f(x)\,dx+\int_c^b f(x)\,dx=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
$$
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="c doesn't need to lie between a and b">
The contiguous-range rule holds for any $c$, not just $a<c<b$ — it follows directly from $F(b)-F(a) = \bigl(F(c)-F(a)\bigr)+\bigl(F(b)-F(c)\bigr)$, which is true regardless of where $c$ sits on the number line (as long as $f$ is defined there).
</Tip>

## MM7.5 The trapezium rule

<FormulaCard title="Trapezium rule">
For $n$ strips of equal width $h=\dfrac{b-a}{n}$, with $y_k=f(a+kh)$:

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \approx \frac h2\bigl(y_0+2y_1+2y_2+\cdots+2y_{n-1}+y_n\bigr)
$$
</FormulaCard>

Each interior $y_k$ is shared between two adjacent trapezia (hence the factor of 2); only the two end values $y_0$ and $y_n$ appear once.

<Tip title="Judging over- or under-estimate from the curve's shape">
If the curve is convex (bulging away from the chord — "concave up," $f''(x)>0$) on the interval, the straight trapezium edges sit *above* the curve, so the rule **overestimates** the area. If the curve is concave ("concave down," $f''(x)<0$), the trapezia sit *below* the curve and the rule **underestimates**. If the curve changes concavity within the interval, you often can't tell without further work.
</Tip>

## MM7.6 Solving dy/dx = f(x)

<WorkedExample title="Solving a differential equation with a boundary condition">
Given $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=3x^2+4x-3$ and $y=5$ when $x=1$, find $y$.

Integrate both sides with respect to $x$:

$$
y = x^3+2x^2-3x+c
$$

Substitute $x=1,\ y=5$: $\ 5=1+2-3+c\ \Rightarrow\ c=5$, so

$$
y = x^3+2x^2-3x+5
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Use definite-integral limits to skip finding c explicitly">
Instead of integrating to find $c$ then substituting, you can integrate directly between the matching pairs of limits: $\displaystyle\int_5^y d y = \int_1^x (3t^2+4t-3)\,dt$, giving $y-5=(x^3+2x^2-3x)-(1+2-3)$ in one line — the same answer without ever writing $+c$.
</Shortcut>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- $\displaystyle\int kx^n\,dx=\dfrac{kx^{n+1}}{n+1}+c$ for $n\ne-1$; simplify to a sum of powers of $x$ first, and don't forget $+c$ on indefinite integrals.
- A definite integral sums signed areas (positive above the axis, negative below) — it is **not** the same as "the area enclosed" unless the curve stays on one side of the axis throughout.
- To find true area when a curve crosses the axis: split at each root, integrate each piece, add the absolute values.
- Odd function on $[-a,a]$: integral is $0$. Even function: integral is $2\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x)\,dx$.
- $\displaystyle\int_a^b f\,dx=-\int_b^a f\,dx$; $\displaystyle\int_a^c f\,dx+\int_c^b f\,dx=\int_a^b f\,dx$ for any $c$.
- Trapezium rule: $\dfrac h2(y_0+2y_1+\cdots+2y_{n-1}+y_n)$ — overestimates on convex (concave-up) curves, underestimates on concave (concave-down) curves.
- $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)$ is solved by integrating $f(x)$; use a boundary condition to pin down $c$.

m2/sequences-and-series.title: Sequences and Series
m2/sequences-and-series.content:
## MM2.1 Sequences, nth-term formulae, and recurrence relations

A **sequence** is an ordered list of numbers; a **series** is the sum of a sequence. A sequence can be defined either by a formula for the $n$th term, or by a **recurrence relation** that builds each term from earlier ones, e.g. $x_{n+1}=f(x_n)$.

<Trap title="Don't assume a pattern from too few terms">
For $x_0=1,\ x_1=2,\ x_{n+2}=|x_n-x_{n+1}|$, the first four terms are $1,2,1,1$ — tempting to guess it repeats "$1,2,1$" forever. But each term depends on the *previous two* terms, so you need to see a repeated **pair** of adjacent terms before concluding the pattern repeats. Writing out more terms here actually gives $1,2,1,1,0,1,1,0,1,1,\ldots$ — a repeating block of 3, not 3 as first guessed.
</Trap>

<Shortcut title="Sum a periodic sequence in blocks">
If a recurrence produces a repeating block (e.g. every 3 terms), split the sum into full blocks plus a short leftover, and watch the ends carefully — $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{100}x_n$ has $101$ terms, not 100, since it includes both endpoints (a classic "fence-post" counting slip).
</Shortcut>

## MM2.2 Arithmetic series

<FormulaCard title="Arithmetic progression (AP)">
$$
u_n = a+(n-1)d
$$

$$
S_n = \frac n2\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr) = \frac n2(u_1+u_n) = n\times(\text{average term})
$$

where $a$ is the first term and $d=u_{n+1}-u_n$ is the common difference.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Sum to n terms">
Find the sum of the first 20 terms of $3,7,11,15,\ldots$

Here $a=3,\ d=4,\ n=20$:

$$
S_{20} = \frac{20}{2}\bigl(2(3)+19(4)\bigr) = 10(6+76) = 820
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Sn = number of terms × average term">
$S_n=n\times\dfrac{u_1+u_n}{2}$ is often the fastest route: find the first and last term, average them, and multiply by how many terms there are — no need to recall the $2a+(n-1)d$ form at all.
</Shortcut>

Adding two arithmetic series term-by-term (or taking any linear combination $\alpha u_n+\beta v_n$) always produces another arithmetic series, with first term and common difference combined the same way.

## MM2.3 Geometric series, and sum to infinity

<FormulaCard title="Geometric progression (GP)">
$$
u_n = ar^{n-1}, \qquad S_n = \frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}, \qquad S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r} \ \ (\text{valid only for } |r|<1)
$$

The ratio of consecutive terms is constant: $\dfrac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}=r$.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Sum to infinity">
Find $S_\infty$ for $8,4,2,1,\ldots$

$$
a=8,\ r=\frac12 \ \Rightarrow\ S_\infty = \frac{8}{1-\frac12} = 16
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Sum to infinity only exists when |r| < 1">
If $|r|\ge1$ the terms don't shrink to zero, so the series has no finite sum — always check $|r|<1$ before using $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$, especially when $r$ is given as an expression that could be $\ge1$ for some values.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Summing a 'slice' of a GP (not the first n terms)">
For $S_k=a+ar+ar^2+\cdots+ar^{k-1}$, find $ar^m+ar^{m+1}+\cdots+ar^n$ (with $n>m$).

Factor out $ar^m$ and treat the bracket as a fresh GP starting at 1:

$$
ar^m+ar^{m+1}+\cdots+ar^n = ar^m\left(1+r+\cdots+r^{n-m}\right) = ar^m\times\frac{1-r^{n-m+1}}{1-r}
$$

Note there are $n-m+1$ terms here, **not** $n-m$ — count a small example on your fingers if unsure (e.g. $r^2$ to $r^4$ is 3 terms: $r^2,r^3,r^4$).
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="New GPs from an old one">
Replacing $r$ by $-r$ in a GP gives another GP with the same first term and ratio $-r$. Taking every other term of a GP (e.g. $a+ar^2+ar^4+\cdots$) gives a GP with ratio $r^2$. Raising every term of a GP to a power $k$ gives a GP with first term $a^k$ and ratio $r^k$. Recognising these patterns turns "derived series" questions into direct substitutions into the standard formulae.
</Shortcut>

## MM2.4 The binomial expansion, n! and (n choose r)

<FormulaCard title="Binomial expansion">
$$
(a+f(x))^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}a^{n-k}\bigl[f(x)\bigr]^k, \qquad \binom{n}{r} = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}
$$

The powers of the two terms in each piece of the expansion always add to $n$, and $\dbinom{n}{r}=\dbinom{n}{n-r}$.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Finding a single term without expanding everything">
Find the term in $x^7$ in $(3+2x)^8$.

Since we need $x^7$, that term must come from $(2x)^7$; the remaining power of $3$ must make the powers add to 8, so it's $3^1$. The binomial coefficient uses $n=8$ and either power, $r=7$ or $r=1$ (they're equal):

$$
\binom{8}{7}\,3^1(2x)^7 = 8\times3\times128\,x^7 = 3072x^7
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Raise the whole term to the power, including its sign and coefficient">
For the coefficient of $x^5$ in $(2-3x)^7$, the term is $\dbinom{7}{5}2^2(-3x)^5$ — **not** $\dbinom{7}{5}2^2 3^5x^5$. Both the $-1$ and the $3$ inside $(-3x)$ must be raised to the power of 5, giving a negative coefficient. Forgetting the bracket around $-3x$ is the single most common binomial-expansion error.
</Trap>

<Shortcut title="Read off n, r, and the two powers directly from the target term">
For the $x^k$ term in $(a+bx)^n$: the power on $bx$ is $k$, the power on $a$ is $n-k$ (they must sum to $n$), and $\dbinom{n}{k}$ (or equivalently $\dbinom{n}{n-k}$) is the coefficient — no need to write out the general sigma formula each time.
</Shortcut>

<Tip title="(n choose r) counts unordered selections">
$\dbinom{n}{r}=\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}$ counts the number of ways to choose $r$ objects from $n$ without caring about order — $\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$ counts *ordered* selections, and dividing by $r!$ removes the $r!$ different orderings of each selected group. This is also why $\dbinom nr=\dbinom{n}{n-r}$: choosing $r$ objects to keep is the same as choosing $n-r$ objects to discard.
</Tip>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- AP: $u_n=a+(n-1)d$, $S_n=\dfrac n2(u_1+u_n)$.
- GP: $u_n=ar^{n-1}$, $S_n=\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$, $S_\infty=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ only when $|r|<1$.
- A "slice" $ar^m+\cdots+ar^n$ has $n-m+1$ terms — factor out $ar^m$ and treat the rest as a fresh GP.
- Binomial: $(a+f(x))^n=\sum\binom nk a^{n-k}[f(x)]^k$, with $\binom nr=\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}=\binom{n}{n-r}$.
- In a binomial term, raise the *entire* bracketed expression (sign, coefficient, and variable) to its power — never split it apart.
- Watch for fence-post errors: count terms/indices on a small example before trusting a formula's limits.

m2/trigonometry.title: Trigonometry
m2/trigonometry.content:
## MM4.1 The sine rule, cosine rule, and area of a triangle

Label a triangle with capital letters at the corners (angles) and matching lower-case letters on the sides opposite them.

<FormulaCard title="Area, sine rule, and cosine rule">
$$
\text{Area} = \frac12 ab\sin C
$$

$$
\frac{\sin A}{a} = \frac{\sin B}{b} = \frac{\sin C}{c} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}
$$

$$
a^2 = b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \cos A = \frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}
$$
</FormulaCard>

The area formula $\frac12ab\sin C$ comes from base $a$ and vertical height $b\sin C$. Rotating which side is the "base" gives $\frac12ab\sin C=\frac12bc\sin A=\frac12ca\sin B$ — three equal expressions for the same area, which rearranges directly into the sine rule. The cosine rule is Pythagoras with a correction term for non-right angles; setting $A=90°$ recovers $a^2=b^2+c^2$ exactly.

| You're given | Use | Find |
|---|---|---|
| Two angles and one side | Sine rule | Any other side (third angle from angles summing to $180°$) |
| Two sides and a non-included angle | Sine rule | Another angle — **may be ambiguous** |
| Three sides | Cosine rule | Any angle |
| Two sides and the included angle | Cosine rule | The third side |

<Trap title="The ambiguous case: two sides and a non-included angle can give two triangles">
In triangle $ABC$, $A=30°$, $b=6$, $a=4$. The sine rule gives $\sin\theta=\dfrac{6\sin30°}{4}=\dfrac34$, so $\theta=48.6°$ **or** $\theta=180°-48.6°=131.4°$. Both are valid here since either, added to the known $30°$, stays under $180°$. Always check whether the obtuse solution is geometrically possible before discarding it — don't assume the calculator's answer is the only one.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Cosine rule for an angle from three sides">
A triangle has $a=7,\ b=8,\ c=5$. Find angle $A$.

$$
\cos A = \frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc} = \frac{64+25-49}{2(8)(5)} = \frac{40}{80} = \frac12 \ \Rightarrow\ A=60°
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Tip title="Right-angled triangle? Use Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA, not the sine/cosine rules">
The sine and cosine rules always work, but if you can see a right angle, plain Pythagoras and basic trig ratios are faster and less error-prone — save the triangle rules for triangles that genuinely aren't right-angled.
</Tip>

## MM4.2 Radians, arc length, and sector area

A radian is the angle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius. One full revolution is $2\pi$ radians $=360°$.

<FormulaCard title="Degree/radian conversion, arc length, sector area">
$$
\theta\text{ degrees} = \frac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi \text{ radians}, \qquad \alpha\text{ radians} = \frac{\alpha}{2\pi}\times360 \text{ degrees}
$$

For a sector of angle $\alpha$ radians in a circle of radius $r$:

$$
\text{arc length} = r\alpha, \qquad \text{area of sector} = \frac12 r^2\alpha
$$
</FormulaCard>

Both formulas fall out of "$\alpha$ radians is a $\dfrac{\alpha}{2\pi}$ fraction of the full circle": arc length $=2\pi r\times\dfrac{\alpha}{2\pi}=r\alpha$; sector area $=\pi r^2\times\dfrac{\alpha}{2\pi}=\frac12r^2\alpha$.

<WorkedExample title="Standard angle conversions">

| Degrees | $30°$ | $45°$ | $60°$ | $90°$ | $180°$ | $360°$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Radians | $\frac{\pi}{6}$ | $\frac{\pi}{4}$ | $\frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ | $\pi$ | $2\pi$ |

Learn this table directly rather than converting each time.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Calculus identities like d/dx(sin x) = cos x only hold in radians">
Any question mixing trigonometry with differentiation or integration assumes the angle is in radians unless stated otherwise — working in degrees would introduce an extra constant factor and break the standard derivative/integral rules.
</Trap>

## MM4.3 Exact values for 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°

<WorkedExample title="Exact trig values from two standard triangles">
$45°$ comes from an isosceles right-angled triangle with legs 1 and hypotenuse $\sqrt2$. $30°$ and $60°$ come from bisecting an equilateral triangle of side 2, giving a right-angled triangle with sides $1,\sqrt3,2$.

| $\theta$ | $0°$ | $30°$ | $45°$ | $60°$ | $90°$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin\theta$ | $0$ | $\frac12$ | $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $\cos\theta$ | $1$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | $\frac12$ | $0$ |
| $\tan\theta$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3$ | undefined |
</WorkedExample>

## MM4.4 Graphs of sine, cosine, and tangent

$\sin$ and $\cos$ repeat every $360°$ ($2\pi$) and oscillate between $-1$ and $1$; $\tan$ repeats every $180°$ ($\pi$) and is undefined at $90°,270°,\ldots$ (where $\cos\theta=0$).

<Shortcut title="Think of sin and cos as projections">
Draw a line of fixed positive length at angle $\theta$ from the origin: $\cos\theta$ is its projection onto the $x$-axis, $\sin\theta$ its projection onto the $y$-axis. This is exactly the CAST diagram in disguise — it immediately tells you the sign of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ in each quadrant without memorising a rule.
</Shortcut>

<WorkedExample title="Reading transformations off the graph">
For $y=\sin\left(2x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$: the coefficient 2 halves the period (compresses horizontally by factor 2), and the phase shift is found by solving $2x+\frac\pi6=0$, i.e. a shift of $-\frac{\pi}{12}$ — always factor out the coefficient of $x$ first to read off the shift correctly: $2\left(x+\frac{\pi}{12}\right)$.
</WorkedExample>

## MM4.5 $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ and $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$

<FormulaCard title="The core trig identities">
$$
\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}, \qquad \sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta \equiv 1
$$

Both hold for **every** angle $\theta$, not just acute ones in a right-angled triangle.
</FormulaCard>

$\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ is Pythagoras' theorem applied to $\sin\theta=\frac OH$ and $\cos\theta=\frac AH$ with $H=1$; $\tan\theta=\frac OA=\frac{O/H}{A/H}=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ follows immediately from the same two definitions.

<Shortcut title="Rearranged forms of the Pythagorean identity">
$\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta\equiv1$ rearranges to $\cos^2\theta\equiv1-\sin^2\theta$ or $\sin^2\theta\equiv1-\cos^2\theta$ — use whichever substitution turns a mixed sin/cos equation into a quadratic in a single function.
</Shortcut>

## MM4.6 Solving trigonometric equations

<WorkedExample title="Squared trig equation — find ALL solutions before rearranging">
Solve $\sin^2(2x+60°)=\dfrac14$ for $-360°<x<360°$.

Take the square root of both sides (both signs): $\sin(2x+60°)=\pm\frac12$.

For $\sin(2x+60°)=\frac12$: the basic solution is $2x+60°=30°$. **Before** isolating $x$, list every solution of $2x+60°$ that could map into range once divided by 2 and shifted by $-60°$:

$$
2x+60° = -690°,-570°,-330°,-210°,30°,150°,390°,510°,750°,870°
$$

Now solve for $x$ and keep only those inside $-360°<x<360°$:

$$
x = -315°,-195°,-135°,-15°,45°,165°,225°,345°
$$

Repeat for $\sin(2x+60°)=-\frac12$ to get the remaining solutions.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Rearranging to x before listing all general solutions loses answers">
If you solve $2x+60°=30°\Rightarrow x=-15°$ first and *then* try to generate other solutions for $x$ by adding $360°$, you'll miss solutions — because the period of $2x+60°$ maps to a period of only $180°$ in $x$, not $360°$. Always list the general solutions in terms of the *original* argument, then divide/shift to isolate $x$ last.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Converting a mixed sin/cos equation into a single-function quadratic">
Solve $12\cos^2x+6\sin x-10=2$ for $0°<x<360°$.

Substitute $\cos^2x=1-\sin^2x$, and let $S=\sin x$:

$$
12(1-S^2)+6S-10=2 \ \Rightarrow\ 12S^2-6S=0 \ \Rightarrow\ 6S(2S-1)=0
$$

$$
S=0 \text{ or } S=\frac12 \ \Rightarrow\ x = 30°,\ 150°,\ 180°
$$

(Note $x=0°$ and $x=360°$ are excluded by the strict inequality — always check the boundary against the given interval.)
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Spot which identity to substitute by looking for a lone sin or cos">
If an equation has $\cos^2x$ alongside a lone $\sin x$ term (or vice versa), substitute $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$ to eliminate whichever function appears only squared, leaving a normal quadratic in the other.
</Shortcut>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- Area: $\frac12ab\sin C$. Sine rule: $\dfrac{\sin A}{a}=\dfrac{\sin B}{b}=\dfrac{\sin C}{c}$. Cosine rule: $a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$.
- Two sides + non-included angle (sine rule) can give **two** valid triangles — check both.
- Radians: arc length $=r\alpha$, sector area $=\frac12r^2\alpha$. $180°=\pi$ rad.
- Learn exact sin/cos/tan for $0°,30°,45°,60°,90°$ from the two standard triangles.
- $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta\equiv1$ — hold for every angle, not just acute ones.
- When solving $\sin(f(x))=k$ etc., list all general solutions for the *argument* first, then isolate $x$ last — rearranging too early loses solutions.
- Mixed $\sin$/$\cos$ equations: substitute the Pythagorean identity to get a quadratic in one function.

</PracticeLink>

physics/electricity.title: Electricity
physics/electricity.content:
## P1.1 Charging by friction and by induction

Rubbing two insulators together (a duster on plastic, fuel through a pipe, a plane through the air) can leave both objects electrically charged. This works for insulators because any charge that builds up stays put. Conductors can charge too, but only if they're insulated from their surroundings — otherwise the charge just leaks away.

<Tip title="It's always electrons that move">
Charging by friction transfers **electrons**, never protons — protons sit deep in the nucleus and are far too tightly bound to hop between objects. An object that loses electrons ends up positive (more protons than electrons left over); one that gains electrons ends up negative. Total charge is conserved, so one object charges positive exactly as much as the other charges negative.
</Tip>

Which way the electrons move depends on which material grips its electrons more strongly — the atoms that hold on tighter end up with the spare electrons (negative), and the other material ends up positive.

Objects can also become charged **by induction**, without ever touching a charged object. Bring a charged object close to a neutral one and the free charges in the neutral object rearrange: opposite charge is pulled towards the near side, like charge is pushed to the far side. If the far side is momentarily earthed while the charged object stays nearby, that repelled charge drains away to Earth — and when the connection to Earth is broken, the object is left with a permanent, opposite charge. This is exactly why a neutral scrap of paper gets pulled towards a charged balloon: induction gives the paper an opposite charge on its near side, and opposite charges attract.

<WorkedExample title="Charging a balloon by friction">
An uncharged rubber balloon is rubbed with a cloth. It becomes negatively charged and stays charged.

Rubbing transfers electrons from the cloth to the balloon, so the balloon ends up with more electrons than protons — an overall negative charge. It *stays* charged because rubber is an insulator: even if part of the balloon touches your (earthed) hand, the charge has no conducting path to escape along.
</WorkedExample>

## P1.2 Forces between charges

<FormulaCard title="Like and unlike charges">
Like charges (+ with +, or − with −) **repel**. Unlike charges (+ with −) **attract**. The force gets bigger with bigger charges and smaller with bigger separation.
</FormulaCard>

This single rule explains a surprising range of everyday electrostatic hazards and party tricks. Touch a positively-charged Van de Graaff dome while standing on an insulating stool, and electrons drain from you into the dome — leaving you (and every strand of your hair) positively charged. Every hair now repels every other hair, so they stand on end. Stand on the ground instead of an insulating stool, and electrons would keep flowing up from Earth to replace the ones you lost, so no charge (and no hair-raising) would build up.

<Trap title="Conductors can't really charge each other by friction">
Two insulators rubbed together stay charged because the charge has nowhere to go. Two conductors in principle could transfer charge the same way, but as soon as they separate, any imbalance instantly equalises through their free electrons (and while they're still touching, they're effectively one object). In practice, meaningful friction charging needs at least one insulator.
</Trap>

## P1.3 Sparking, hazards, and earthing

Sparking happens when the voltage between two charged objects gets big enough (or the gap small enough) to ionise the air between them, letting a sudden discharge jump across. Small sparks are just a nuisance — static shocks from a car door or a nylon carpet. Large sparks, though, are a genuine fire and explosion risk wherever there's flammable vapour around, which is exactly the situation during aircraft refuelling: fuel rushing through a pipe generates friction, friction charges the fuel and the pipe, and a spark near the fuel tank could ignite the vapour.

<Shortcut title="Earthing prevents charge building up in the first place">
Connecting two objects together (or connecting one to Earth) with a wire gives any charge a path to drain away as fast as it's generated, so no charge imbalance — and no spark risk — ever builds up. This is why fuel tanks and refuelling pipes are always earthed before fuel starts flowing, and it's the standard fix whenever a question asks how to eliminate a described sparking hazard.
</Shortcut>

<WorkedExample title="Electrostatic paint spraying">
Paint droplets leave a spray gun positively charged; the car body is earthed. Which of these are true: (1) droplets attract each other, (2) droplets attract the panel, (3) droplets can reach parts not directly in the line of the spray, (4) the panel gradually becomes positively charged?

All the droplets carry the *same* sign of charge, so they **repel** each other — statement 1 is false, but this repulsion is actually the useful part, since it keeps the spray spread out into an even coat instead of clumping.

As a droplet approaches the earthed panel, it induces an opposite (negative) charge on the metal surface near it, so the droplet is attracted in — statement 2 is true. That same induced attraction can pull droplets around the edge of a panel onto surfaces not in a direct line from the gun — statement 3 is true.

Because the panel is earthed, any positive charge deposited by droplets is immediately neutralised by electrons flowing in from Earth, so the panel itself never builds up a net charge — statement 4 is false.
</WorkedExample>

## P1.4 Circuit symbols, and ac vs dc

You should be able to recognise and draw the standard symbols for a cell, battery, lamp, resistor, variable resistor, ammeter, voltmeter, switch, and diode, and know that an ammeter goes **in series** with the component it measures while a voltmeter goes **in parallel** across it.

<FormulaCard title="Direct vs alternating current">
**Direct current (dc)** always flows the same way — the output of a cell or battery. **Alternating current (ac)** repeatedly reverses direction, typically in a smooth sine-wave pattern — the output of a generator, and of UK mains at 50 Hz (50 complete cycles per second).
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="A changing current isn't automatically alternating">
Alternating current must actually reverse direction — its waveform has to dip below the axis as well as rise above it, not just wobble in size while staying positive. A current that varies in magnitude but never changes sign is still dc.
</Trap>

<Tip title="Diodes turn ac into dc">
A diode only lets current through in one direction (the way its arrow points), so a diode — or a set of them wired as a "rectifier" — can convert the ac from a mains supply into dc.
</Tip>

## P1.5 Conductors and insulators

Metals, graphite, and ionic solutions conduct well because they contain charge carriers (free electrons in metals, ions in solution) that can move through the material. Most non-metals — plastics, rubber, dry wood, air — are good insulators, because their electrons are all bound up and can't drift through the bulk material.

<Trap title="Water is a conductor, not an insulator">
Pure water is actually a fairly poor conductor, but any water with dissolved ions in it (which is essentially all water you'll meet outside a lab) conducts well. So "wet" or "damp" materials shouldn't be treated as insulators, even if the dry material normally would be — this is exactly why a bathroom light switch is operated by a nylon pull-cord rather than a switch you touch directly: condensation on a normal switch could conduct a shock straight to you, while the insulating, water-resistant nylon cord keeps you safe.
</Trap>

## P1.6 Current, charge, and time

<FormulaCard title="Current">
$$
I = \frac{Q}{t}
$$

Current $I$ (amps, A) is the rate of flow of charge $Q$ (coulombs, C) past a point, over time $t$ (seconds, s). $1\,\text{mA}=10^{-3}\,\text{A}$, $1\,\mu\text{A}=10^{-6}\,\text{A}$.
</FormulaCard>

In a metal, current is carried by free electrons drifting towards the positive terminal — but by (historical) convention, current itself is always described as flowing from positive to negative, i.e. in the *opposite* direction to the electrons actually moving.

<WorkedExample title="Charge from current and time">
A resistor carries a current of 30 mA for 20 s. How much charge passes through it?

$$
Q = It = (30\times10^{-3})\times20 = 0.60\ \text{C}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Current from charge and time">
A charge of 6000 μC passes through a component in 50 minutes. What is the average current?

Convert to base units first: $Q = 6000\times10^{-6}\ \text{C} = 6\times10^{-3}\ \text{C}$, $t = 50\times60 = 3000\ \text{s}$.

$$
I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{6\times10^{-3}}{3000} = 2.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{A} = 2.0\ \mu\text{A}
$$
</WorkedExample>

## P1.7 Resistance, and V–I graphs

<FormulaCard title="Resistance">
$$
R = \frac{V}{I}
$$

Resistance $R$ (ohms, $\Omega$) relates voltage $V$ (volts) and current $I$ (amps). For a component that obeys **Ohm's law** (e.g. a metal wire at constant temperature), $I$ is directly proportional to $V$, so $R$ stays constant regardless of $V$ or $I$.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Rearranging R = V/I">
A resistor carries 60 mA when connected to a 12 V battery. Find its resistance, and then find the current in a 72 MΩ resistor connected across a 1.8 kV supply.

$$
R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{12}{60\times10^{-3}} = 200\ \Omega
$$

$$
I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{1.8\times10^3}{72\times10^6} = 25\times10^{-6}\ \text{A} = 25\ \mu\text{A}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Reading V–I graphs">
For an **ohmic** component (fixed resistor at constant temperature), a $V$–$I$ graph is a straight line through the origin, and $R = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}$ is just its gradient. For a **filament lamp**, resistance rises as it heats up, so the graph curves — steepening as $I$ increases — and you can no longer read $R$ off as a single gradient; instead pick a point and compute $R=V/I$ at *that* point specifically.
</Shortcut>

<Trap title="A curved V–I graph still means R = V/I, just not the gradient">
On a curved graph, the temptation is to differentiate or eyeball a tangent to get "the resistance." Don't — resistance at a point is always the ratio of that point's $V$ to its $I$, found by drawing a straight line from the origin to the point, not by the local slope of the curve.
</Trap>

## P1.8 Thermistors, LDRs, and diodes

<FormulaCard title="Three non-ohmic components">
**NTC thermistor** — resistance *decreases* as temperature *increases*. **LDR (light-dependent resistor)** — resistance *decreases* as light intensity *increases*. **Ideal diode** — (near) zero resistance in the direction its arrow points, (near) infinite resistance the other way.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Thermistor cooling in a circuit">
A circuit has a thermistor (NTC) in series with a fixed resistor and a battery. Ammeter 1 reads the circuit current; voltmeter 2 reads across the thermistor. The thermistor cools down. What happens to each reading?

Cooling makes the thermistor's resistance rise, which raises the total resistance of the (series) circuit, which drops the current — so ammeter 1's reading **falls**. With less current, the fixed resistor claims a smaller share of the battery's fixed total voltage (from $V=IR$ with $R$ constant), so the thermistor's share — and voltmeter 2's reading — **rises**. Notice the resistance increase "wins" against the current decrease here.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Trace which way each diode's arrow points before deciding what lights up">
In a circuit with several diodes and lamps, a lamp only lights if there's an unbroken path of *forward-biased* diodes (arrows pointing from + to − around the loop) in series with it. A single reverse-biased diode anywhere in a branch blocks current for the whole branch, however many correctly-oriented components sit alongside it.
</Trap>

## P1.9 Series and parallel rules

<FormulaCard title="Series circuits">
Same **current** through every component (only one path for charge to take). **Voltages add up** to the supply voltage (each unit of charge shares its energy out across every component it passes through).
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="Parallel circuits">
Same **voltage** across every branch (every unit of charge that goes through, say, branch 1 experiences the full supply voltage). **Currents add up**: total current into a junction equals total current out.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Voltmeter or ammeter? Look at what it's wired across">
A meter with no other component in series with it, sitting across a component, is a voltmeter. A meter directly in the main path of the current, in series with a component, is an ammeter — even if at a glance it looks like it's "parallel" to something else nearby. Trace the wires carefully around parallel branches before deciding.
</Tip>

## P1.10 Combining resistors

<FormulaCard title="Resistors in series">
$$
R_T = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots
$$

Always **bigger** than any individual resistance — every resistor in series adds more opposition to the same current.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="Resistors in parallel">
$$
\frac{1}{R_T} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \cdots
$$

Always **smaller** than the smallest individual resistance — extra parallel branches just give the current extra routes, so the supply can push out more total current for the same voltage.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Series combination">
Two resistors, 2 Ω and 3 Ω, in series, connected to a 10 V supply.

$$
R_T = 2+3 = 5\ \Omega \qquad I = \frac{10}{5} = 2\ \text{A}
$$

Voltage across each: $2\times2=4\ \text{V}$ and $2\times3=6\ \text{V}$ — and indeed $4+6=10\ \text{V}$, the full supply voltage.
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Parallel combination">
Two resistors, 2 Ω and 3 Ω, in parallel, connected to a 6 V supply.

Each resistor feels the full 6 V, so:

$$
I_2 = \frac{6}{2}=3\ \text{A}, \qquad I_3 = \frac{6}{3}=2\ \text{A}, \qquad I_{\text{total}} = 3+2 = 5\ \text{A}
$$

$$
R_T = \frac{V}{I_{\text{total}}} = \frac{6}{5} = 1.2\ \Omega
$$

Comfortably less than either 2 Ω or 3 Ω, as expected.
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Splitting current at a junction, without solving the full circuit">
In a parallel pair, current splits **inversely** to resistance — the branch with less resistance carries proportionally more current. If one branch has twice the resistance of the other, it carries half the current. This lets you find individual branch currents quickly once you know the total, without recomputing $I=V/R$ for each branch from scratch.
</Shortcut>

## P1.11 Voltage as energy per charge

<FormulaCard title="Voltage">
$$
V = \frac{E}{Q}
$$

Voltage (volts, $1\,\text{V}=1\,\text{J}\,\text{C}^{-1}$) is the energy $E$ transferred per unit charge $Q$ passing through a component.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Current is about rate, voltage is about energy per charge — don't mix them up">
Current tells you how fast charge is moving round the circuit. Voltage tells you how much energy each unit of that charge hands over (or picks up) at a particular component. That distinction is exactly why current is shared equally in series but voltage is shared out, while voltage is shared equally in parallel but current is shared out.
</Tip>

## P1.12 Power and energy

<FormulaCard title="Electrical power">
$$
P = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}
$$

All three forms follow from $P=VI$ combined with $V=IR$ — pick whichever form uses the two quantities you already know.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="Energy transferred">
$$
E = Pt = VIt
$$

Energy (joules) is power (watts) times time (seconds) — make sure $V$, $I$, and $t$ are all in base SI units (volts, amps, seconds) before multiplying.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Combining series/parallel with power and energy">
A 3 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor are in parallel; that combination is in series with a 4 Ω resistor, all connected to an 18 V supply. The 4 Ω resistor dissipates 36 W. Find the energy dissipated in the 6 Ω resistor in 1 minute.

Current through the 4 Ω resistor (which carries the *total* current, since it's before the split):

$$
I = \sqrt{\frac{P}{R}} = \sqrt{\frac{36}{4}} = 3\ \text{A}
$$

The 3 Ω branch has half the resistance of the 6 Ω branch, so it carries twice the current: splitting 3 A in that ratio gives 2 A through the 3 Ω resistor and 1 A through the 6 Ω resistor.

$$
V_{6\Omega} = IR = 1\times6 = 6\ \text{V}
$$

$$
E = VIt = 6\times1\times60 = 360\ \text{J}
$$
</WorkedExample>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- Friction and induction charging both work by moving **electrons** only; charge is always conserved overall.
- Like charges repel, unlike charges attract; earthing drains charge away as it forms, preventing sparking hazards.
- dc flows one way; ac reverses direction — UK mains is ac at 50 Hz.
- $I=\dfrac{Q}{t}$; $R=\dfrac{V}{I}$ (constant for ohmic components, not constant for filament lamps, thermistors, LDRs).
- NTC thermistor: resistance ↓ as temperature ↑. LDR: resistance ↓ as light ↑. Diode: conducts one way only.
- Series: same current, voltages add. Parallel: same voltage, currents add.
- $R_T=R_1+R_2+\cdots$ in series (always bigger); $\dfrac{1}{R_T}=\dfrac1{R_1}+\dfrac1{R_2}+\cdots$ in parallel (always smaller).
- $V=\dfrac{E}{Q}$; $P=VI=I^2R=\dfrac{V^2}{R}$; $E=Pt=VIt$.
