</PracticeLink>

physics/magnetism.title: Magnetism
physics/magnetism.content:
## P2.1 Poles, attraction and repulsion

Every permanent magnet has two poles, north (N) and south (S) — you can't get a magnet with just one pole, however small you cut it up. The rule for how poles interact is simple:

<FormulaCard title="Like and unlike poles">
**Like poles repel** (N–N or S–S). **Unlike poles attract** (N–S). The force gets stronger the closer the poles are, and weaker as they move apart — exactly the same shape of behaviour as the force between electric charges.
</FormulaCard>

A magnet will also attract unmagnetised pieces of magnetic material (iron, cobalt, nickel), regardless of which pole you use — this is because bringing either pole close *induces* an opposite pole in the material (more on that below).

<Trap title="Attraction alone doesn't prove something is a magnet">
If object A pulls object B towards it, that's consistent with A being a magnet and B being unmagnetised iron — or with both being magnets. To *prove* A is a genuinely magnetised object (not just magnetic material), you need to show it **repels** a known pole of another magnet. Repulsion can only ever happen between two magnets; attraction happens either way.
</Trap>

<Tip title="Compass needles seek Earth's poles">
The "north" end of a compass needle is really its north-*seeking* pole — it points towards the Earth's north geographic pole. Confusingly, that means the Earth's north geographic pole is actually a magnetic *south* pole (since unlike poles attract), and vice versa at the south.
</Tip>

## P2.2 The magnetic field around a bar magnet

A magnetic field is the region of space around a magnet in which it can exert a force on other magnets or magnetic materials. We draw it as field lines.

<FormulaCard title="Rules for drawing magnetic field lines">
- Lines run from **north to south** outside the magnet (they never start or end in mid-air — they either run pole-to-pole or form closed loops).
- Lines never cross each other.
- The **direction** of a line at any point is the direction a free north pole would be pushed if placed there.
- Lines drawn **closer together** mean a **stronger** field; that's why the field is always strongest right next to the poles.
</FormulaCard>

Two everyday ways to actually see this pattern: sprinkle iron filings on a card laid over the magnet (each filing becomes a tiny induced magnet and lines up along the field, tracing out the shape but *not* telling you which end is north), or walk a small plotting compass around the magnet step by step, drawing an arrow each time it settles (this gives you direction too, but not field strength).

<WorkedExample title="Reading a field pattern between two magnets">
Iron filings scattered near two bar magnets form a pattern with a region of almost no filings at point A (between the two facing poles) and a region of dense, reinforcing lines at point B. Is the force between the magnets attraction or repulsion?

At A the field is very weak — that only happens if the two poles' field lines point in *opposite* directions there and cancel out, which means the two facing poles are the **same** (both N or both S). At B, the lines from each pole add up rather than cancel, confirming they're pointing the same way — consistent with two like poles facing each other. Like poles repel, so this is a **repulsion**.
</WorkedExample>

## P2.3 Soft and hard magnetic materials

<FormulaCard title="Soft vs hard magnetic materials">
**Soft** magnetic materials (e.g. iron) magnetise **and** demagnetise easily — good for anything that needs to switch its magnetism on and off quickly. **Hard** magnetic materials (e.g. steel) are difficult to magnetise, but once magnetised they hold onto it — good for permanent magnets.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="'Soft' and 'hard' here have nothing to do with mechanical hardness">
Steel is mechanically harder than iron in the everyday sense, but magnetically it's the "hard" material precisely because it *resists* changing its magnetic state — hard to magnetise, hard to demagnetise. Don't let the everyday meaning of the words pull you towards the wrong material when a question asks which is "harder" to work with.
</Trap>

This split explains a lot of design choices you'll be asked to justify. A compass needle needs to hold its magnetism for years without a reset, so it's made from a **hard** material. The core inside an electromagnet needs to magnetise the instant current flows and lose it the instant current stops — so it's made from a **soft** material (iron), letting the whole electromagnet be switched on and off cleanly.

## P2.4 Induced magnetism

<Tip title="Induced magnetism is always attractive, never repulsive">
Bring either pole of a magnet near an unmagnetised piece of magnetic material and it induces the *opposite* pole on the near surface — a north pole induces a south pole facing it, and vice versa. Since opposite poles attract, there's *never* a repulsive force here, whichever pole you use. If two objects repel each other, at least one of them must already be a permanent magnet.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Working out what two attracting cylinders could be">
Cylinders X and Y attract each other whichever pair of ends you bring together. Which is possible: (1) both are magnets, (2) X is a magnet and Y is unmagnetised iron, (3) Y is a magnet and X is unmagnetised iron, (4) both are unmagnetised iron?

If both X and Y were magnets, then *some* orientation would bring two like poles together and they'd repel — but they attract in every orientation, so (1) is ruled out. If both were unmagnetised iron, neither could exert any magnetic force at all, so (4) is ruled out too. But one magnet plus one piece of unmagnetised iron always attracts, regardless of which end faces which (the iron's near pole is always induced to be opposite to whatever pole approaches it) — so both (2) and (3) remain genuinely possible; there's no way to tell which object is the real magnet from this test alone.
</WorkedExample>

This same effect — inducing poles with an external field — is how permanent magnets get made in the first place: a hard magnetic material is placed inside a strong field (typically from a solenoid) until it becomes permanently magnetised itself.

## P2.5 The magnetic effect of a current

Electric currents create their own magnetic fields, entirely separate from any permanent magnet. You can demonstrate this with nothing more than a wire and a compass: run a wire north-south, place a compass directly underneath, and switch the current on — the needle deflects away from north. Switch it off, and it swings back.

<FormulaCard title="What affects the current's magnetic field">
**Reversing the current's direction** reverses the direction of the field (the compass deflects the other way). **Increasing the current** increases the field strength (bigger deflection). Note it's the *moving charge itself* that creates the field, not the wire material — a beam of electrons in a vacuum creates exactly the same kind of field.
</FormulaCard>

## P2.6 Field patterns: straight wires, coils, and solenoids

<FormulaCard title="Straight wire">
Concentric circles centred on the wire, getting further apart (weaker field) the further from the wire. Direction given by the **right-hand grip rule**: point your right thumb along the direction of conventional current, and your curled fingers show the direction of the field circles.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Iron filings around a current-carrying wire">
A card is threaded onto a long straight wire, perpendicular to it, and iron filings are sprinkled on top while a current flows. What pattern forms?

The filings settle into **concentric circles** centred on the wire, exactly matching the field-line pattern — packed closely together right next to the wire (strong field) and spreading out further from it (weaker field).
</WorkedExample>

<FormulaCard title="Coils and solenoids">
Winding the wire into a coil makes the field from every turn add together through the middle, producing one strong, fairly uniform field down the axis — very similar in shape to a bar magnet's field, with one end acting as a north pole and the other as south. The direction is still found with the right-hand grip rule, curling your fingers the way the current flows round each turn; your thumb then points out of the north end.
</FormulaCard>

<Shortcut title="Clockwise-anticlockwise trick for solenoid ends">
Look end-on at a coil, in the direction the current is circulating. **Clockwise** current (as you view it) means that end is a **south** pole; **anticlockwise** means **north**. A handy mnemonic: anticlockwise loosely traces the shape of an "N", clockwise loosely traces an "S".
</Shortcut>

<WorkedExample title="Finding the north end of a coil">
A coil is connected to a dc supply with terminal A on the positive side and B on the negative side. Which end acts as the north pole?

Current flows from positive to negative, so around the coil it flows from A towards B. Applying the right-hand grip rule (or checking whether the current circulates clockwise or anticlockwise when viewed from each end) shows the field lines emerge from the end nearest **A** — so that's the north pole.
</WorkedExample>

## P2.7 Factors affecting field strength around a wire or coil

<FormulaCard title="What makes the field stronger">
- **Bigger current** → stronger field, at a wire, a coil, or a solenoid.
- **Closer to the wire** → stronger field; further away → weaker.
- **A ferromagnetic core** (e.g. soft iron) inside a coil → much stronger field, because the atoms in the core act like tiny magnets that line up with the field and add to it.
- **More turns per unit length** on a solenoid → stronger field.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="An alternating current still obeys all the same rules — moment by moment">
If the current in a wire is ac rather than dc, the field it produces still depends on the current's magnitude and direction at that instant — it's just that both are now continuously changing. So the field around a mains cable is weaker further away (like any current-carrying wire), constantly reversing direction (because the current does), and varying in strength (because the current's magnitude varies too). Don't assume ac "breaks" the normal rules; it just makes every one of them time-dependent.
</Trap>

## P2.8 Permanent magnets vs electromagnets

An electromagnet is just a solenoid wound around a soft iron core — same field shape as a bar magnet, but built from a coil and a current rather than fixed-in magnetic material.

<FormulaCard title="Electromagnet vs permanent magnet">
| | Electromagnet | Permanent magnet |
|---|---|---|
| Can be switched off | Yes (stop the current) | No |
| Strength | Adjustable (via current) | Roughly fixed |
| Polarity | Reversible (reverse the current) | Fixed |
| Core/material | Soft magnetic material | Hard magnetic material |
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Why the core must be soft, not hard">
Explain why the core of an electromagnet is made from a soft, not a hard, magnetic material.

A hard material is difficult to magnetise, so the electromagnet would build up its field only slowly and weakly when switched on. Worse, once magnetised it would *stay* magnetised even after the current is switched off — defeating the entire point of an electromagnet, which is that it needs to switch off completely.
</WorkedExample>

Because they can be switched on and off, varied in strength, and even reversed in polarity, electromagnets are far more flexible than permanent magnets — used everywhere from lifting magnets in scrapyards (soft iron core, thick coil, huge current — released by simply cutting the power) to loudspeakers and relay switches.

## P2.9 The motor effect and Fleming's left-hand rule

<FormulaCard title="The motor effect">
A current-carrying wire placed in a magnetic field experiences a force — **provided** the current isn't parallel to the field. The force is a maximum when current and field are at right angles, and zero when they're parallel. It acts **perpendicular to both** the current and the field — never directly towards or away from either pole.
</FormulaCard>

Physically, this happens because the current's own field (circular loops around the wire) interacts with the external field: on one side of the wire the two fields reinforce, on the other they partly cancel, and the wire gets pushed from the strong side towards the weak side — a bit like squeezing something out from between stretched elastic bands.

<FormulaCard title="Fleming's left-hand rule">
Hold the thumb and first two fingers of your **left** hand mutually at right angles: **F**irst finger = **F**ield (N to S), se**C**ond finger = **C**urrent (+ to −), th**uM**b = **M**otor effect force. Reversing *either* current or field alone reverses the force; reversing *both* leaves the force direction unchanged.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Identifying which parts of a circuit feel a force">
A rectangular loop of wire sits partly inside a uniform magnetic field between the poles of a magnet, with the top and bottom sides of the loop running perpendicular to the field and the right-hand side running parallel to it. Which sides feel a motor effect force, and in what directions?

The motor effect needs current that isn't parallel to the field. The top and bottom sides are perpendicular to the field, so both feel a force — applying the left-hand rule to each (same field direction, opposite current directions on the two sides, since current flows round the loop) gives forces in opposite directions on the two sides. The right-hand side runs parallel to the field, so it feels no motor effect force at all.
</WorkedExample>

## P2.10 Factors affecting the force, and F = BIL

<FormulaCard title="What the force depends on">
- Bigger current → bigger force.
- Stronger field → bigger force.
- More wire length inside the field → bigger force.
- Angle between current and field → force is maximum at 90°, zero at 0°.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="F = BIL">
$$
F = BIL
$$

$F$ = force (N), $B$ = magnetic field strength / flux density (T, tesla), $I$ = current (A), $L$ = length of wire *at right angles to the field* (m). Only valid when the wire is perpendicular to the field — for any other angle you'd only use the perpendicular component of $L$ or $B$.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="1 tesla, defined">
Rearranging gives $B=\dfrac{F}{IL}$: a field of strength 1 T exerts a force of exactly 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A, perpendicular to the field. Units-wise, $1\,\text{T} = 1\,\text{N}\,\text{A}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-1}$.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Rearranging F = BIL">
A wire carries 4.0 A perpendicular to a 0.20 T field, with 0.050 m of its length inside the field. Find the force. Then find the current needed to produce a 0.10 N force on a 0.20 m length of wire in a 0.40 T field.

$$
F = BIL = 0.20\times4.0\times0.050 = 0.040\ \text{N}
$$

$$
I = \frac{F}{BL} = \frac{0.10}{0.40\times0.20} = 1.25\ \text{A}
$$
</WorkedExample>

Put a current-carrying loop in a uniform field and each straight side perpendicular to the field feels a force in an opposite direction to the side facing it — a pair of forces separated by the width of the coil, which is exactly what produces a turning effect (moment). That turning effect is the whole basis of the dc motor.

## P2.11 The dc motor

As the coil rotates, the separation between the two motor-effect forces changes: it's biggest when the coil lies *in* the plane of the field (forces furthest apart, maximum turning effect) and shrinks to zero when the coil is perpendicular to the field (forces in line, zero turning effect) — and just past that point, the turning effect would reverse and push the coil back the way it came, unless something intervenes.

<FormulaCard title="The split-ring commutator">
The **commutator** is a rotating switch, connected to the coil and contacted by fixed carbon **brushes**. Every half-turn, right around the point where the turning effect would otherwise reverse, it swaps which side of the coil is connected to the positive terminal — flipping the current direction in the coil at exactly the right moment so the motor effect force keeps pushing the coil the **same** way round, turn after turn.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="The current in the coil reverses twice per rotation, not once">
It's tempting to think "commutator flips the current once per rotation" because a full rotation feels like one cycle — but the flip happens at *each* of the two vertical crossing points, so the current direction in the coil actually reverses **twice** every full turn.
</Trap>

<FormulaCard title="What makes a dc motor turn faster / harder">
Bigger current, larger coil area, stronger field, more turns on the coil, or winding the coil onto a soft iron core (boosts the field) — all increase the turning effect. The turning effect itself still depends on the coil's angle in the field, maximum in-plane and zero perpendicular, exactly as for a single straight wire.
</FormulaCard>

## P2.12 Applications of electromagnets

The same on/off, adjustable-strength, reversible-polarity toolkit from earlier shows up everywhere:

- **Loudspeakers**: a voice coil sits in a permanent magnet's radial field; feeding it a varying (audio) current makes the motor effect push the coil — and the attached cone — back and forth, producing sound.
- **Lifting magnets**: a thick coil around a soft iron core, switched on to pick up scrap metal by induced attraction, then switched off to drop it — something a permanent magnet simply couldn't do.

<WorkedExample title="Electromagnet vs permanent magnet for lifting scrap">
Give two advantages of using an electromagnet, rather than a permanent magnet, to lift and move heavy steel objects.

First, it can be **switched off** to release the object exactly where you want it — a permanent magnet would need to be physically prised away. Second, its strength can be **varied** by varying the current, letting the same crane handle loads of very different sizes.
</WorkedExample>

## P2.13 Electromagnetic induction: cutting field lines and changing fields

<FormulaCard title="Two ways to induce a voltage">
A voltage is induced in a conductor whenever (1) it **cuts across** magnetic field lines (relative motion between conductor and field), or (2) the magnetic field **passing through it changes** in strength. These aren't really two separate rules — moving a magnet past a coil changes the field through the coil at the same time as the wires cut its field lines, so both descriptions are just two ways of talking about the same physical event.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="No relative motion (or no changing field) means no induced voltage — however strong the field is">
A magnet resting motionless right inside a coil induces nothing at all, no matter how strong it is — induction needs *change*. Two objects moving together at the same velocity (so there's no relative motion between them) also induce nothing, even if both are moving fast relative to the ground.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Spotting which situations induce a voltage">
A bar magnet sits near a coil. In which of these is a voltage induced: (1) magnet moved towards the coil, (2) magnet moved away, (3) coil moved towards the magnet, (4) coil and magnet both moved the same way at the same speed, (5) magnet held stationary inside the coil?

Induction needs the field *through* the coil to change, which needs relative motion between magnet and coil — it doesn't matter which one is "actually" moving. That happens in (1), (2), and (3): a voltage is induced in each. In (4) they move together with no relative motion, and in (5) nothing moves at all — no induced voltage in either case.
</WorkedExample>

A closed circuit is also needed before any of this produces a *current* — with the circuit open, there's still an induced voltage sitting across the terminals, just nothing flowing.

## P2.14 Factors affecting induced voltage: magnitude and direction

<FormulaCard title="Magnitude of the induced voltage">
Directly proportional to the **rate** of cutting field lines, or equivalently the **rate of change** of field through the conductor. Practically: move faster, use a stronger magnet, or add more turns to the coil — any of these increases the induced voltage.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="Direction: Lenz's law">
The induced voltage (and any resulting current) always acts in the direction that **opposes** the change that produced it. Push a magnet's north pole towards a coil, and the coil's near end becomes a north pole too — repelling the approaching magnet and resisting your push. Pull it away, and the near end flips to a south pole, now attracting it back — again resisting the change.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Lenz's law is really just conservation of energy">
If the induced current *helped* the change instead of opposing it, you'd get electrical energy out of the circuit for free, with no work being done anywhere — energy from nothing. Opposing the change means you have to do work (against the repulsion, or against the attraction) to keep the magnet moving, and that mechanical work is exactly what "pays" for the electrical energy generated.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Comparing induced voltage on an aircraft's outward and return flights">
An aircraft's metal wings cut through the vertical part of Earth's magnetic field as it flies. Flying north it induces some voltage across its wingtips; flying south on the return leg it travels faster. How does the return voltage compare, and why?

The induced voltage is proportional to the rate of cutting field lines, and a higher speed means a higher rate of cutting — so the return voltage is **larger** in magnitude. Flying in the opposite direction also reverses which wingtip cuts the field lines "into" versus "out of," so the **polarity reverses** as well.
</WorkedExample>

## P2.15 The ac generator

Spin a coil inside a uniform magnetic field and the field through it is constantly changing direction and rate — inducing a continuously alternating voltage, i.e. an ac generator.

<FormulaCard title="What increases the generator's output">
- **Faster rotation** → higher rate of change of field → bigger peak voltage, and also a **higher frequency** of the output (frequency = rotation frequency).
- **Stronger field**, **larger coil area**, or **more turns** → each increases the rate of change of field (or of cutting field lines) → bigger peak voltage. More turns also just adds several equal induced voltages in series.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Peak voltage occurs when the coil sides move fastest across the field, not when the coil is 'most aligned'">
Picture the coil sides sweeping through the field: voltage is largest when the wires move **perpendicular** to the field lines (cutting them at the fastest possible rate — this happens as the coil passes through the plane of the field) and drops to **zero** when the wires move **parallel** to the field (no cutting at all — this happens as the coil passes through the perpendicular position). It's easy to guess these the wrong way round, so check by picturing the wire's actual velocity relative to the field lines at that instant.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Checking statements about a simple ac generator">
Which of these are correct: (1) reversing the rotation direction still gives an ac output, (2) slip rings and brushes must be conductors, (3) doubling the rotation period doubles the peak voltage and halves the frequency, (4) one slip ring is always positive?

(1) is correct — either direction of rotation, each side of the coil still alternates between moving up and down through the field every half turn, so the output is ac regardless of which way it spins. (2) is correct — current has to actually flow through the brushes and slip rings to reach the external circuit, so both must conduct. (3) is wrong on the voltage: doubling the period means rotating *more slowly*, cutting field lines at a lower rate, so the peak voltage **falls**, not doubles (the frequency *does* halve, since $f=1/T$, but that alone doesn't make the whole statement correct). (4) is wrong: each slip ring's polarity swaps every half rotation, exactly like the coil's induced voltage does.
</WorkedExample>

## P2.16 Applications of electromagnetic induction

Two big ones dominate the specification: **generators** (mechanical energy in, ac electrical energy out — the mechanical energy itself coming from burning fuel to drive steam turbines, or directly from wind/water turbines) and **transformers** (stepping ac voltages up or down for efficient transmission, covered next).

<WorkedExample title="Identifying the energy transfer done by a generator">
A nuclear power station uses a generator to supply the grid. Which energy transfer does the *generator itself* perform: nuclear → electrical, chemical → electrical, kinetic → electrical, or thermal → electrical?

The nuclear reaction heats water to raise steam, and that steam's kinetic energy spins a turbine connected to the generator. The generator's own job — electromagnetic induction turning a spinning coil (or magnet) into an induced voltage — is specifically the **kinetic → electrical** step; everything upstream of the turbine is a separate stage in the chain.
</WorkedExample>

Smaller-scale examples worth knowing: a car alternator recharging the battery while the engine runs, a shake-to-charge torch (shaking a magnet through a coil lights an LED), and induction hobs (an alternating current in a coil under the glass creates a changing field that induces current — and heating — directly in a metal pan placed above it).

## P2.17 Transformers and the turns ratio

A transformer is two coils — **primary** (input side) and **secondary** (output side) — wound onto a shared soft iron core, using electromagnetic induction to step an ac voltage up or down.

<FormulaCard title="Step-up vs step-down">
**Step-up**: more turns on secondary than primary ($n_s>n_p$), so $V_s>V_p$. **Step-down**: fewer turns on secondary ($n_s<n_p$), so $V_s<V_p$.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="Turns ratio = voltage ratio">
$$
\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{n_p}{n_s}
$$

Valid for an **ideal** (100% efficient) transformer — a good approximation for most real transformers used in practice.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="A transformer needs ac — a constant dc current does nothing">
The primary coil's field only induces a voltage in the secondary while it's *changing*. A steady dc current in the primary still creates a magnetic field through the core, but a constant one, so nothing is induced in the secondary at all. This is exactly why every transformer application (mains stepping, long-distance transmission) relies on ac, never dc.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Finding the turns ratio for a step-down transformer">
A transformer steps 240 V ac down to 20 V ac. Which of these turns counts (primary, secondary) is possible: (4800, 400), (400, 4800), (48000, 400), (400, 48000)?

Step-down means fewer turns on the secondary, ruling out any option with more turns on the secondary side. The voltage ratio is $20/240 = 1/12$, so the turns ratio must also be $1:12$ — checking (4800, 400): $4800/400=12$. That's the only option satisfying both the direction (step-down) and the correct ratio.
</WorkedExample>

## P2.18 Transformer power, and power transmission

<FormulaCard title="Power in an ideal transformer">
$$
V_pI_p = V_sI_s
$$

100% efficiency means power in equals power out ($P=VI$ on each side). Rearranging shows the **current** ratio is the *inverse* of the voltage (and turns) ratio: $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{I_s}{I_p}=\dfrac{n_p}{n_s}$ — so whatever a transformer does to voltage, it does the opposite to current.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Finding output current from the power relationship">
A transformer steps up from 25 000 V to 250 000 V, with a 4.0 A input current. Find the output current.

$$
V_pI_p = V_sI_s \ \Rightarrow\ 25\,000\times4.0 = 250\,000\times I_s \ \Rightarrow\ I_s = 0.40\ \text{A}
$$

Voltage stepped up by a factor of 10, so current stepped down by the same factor of 10 — a quick sanity check that doesn't even need the full calculation.
</WorkedExample>

<FormulaCard title="Why transmission uses high voltage">
Transmission cables have resistance $R$, so any current in them wastes power as heat: $P_{\text{wasted}}=I^2R$. Transmitting the *same* power ($P=IV$) at a much **higher voltage** means a much **lower current**, and because the loss depends on $I^2$, even a modest reduction in current gives a much bigger cut in wasted power.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Don't confuse the transmission voltage with the voltage drop along the cable">
The high voltage that's stepped up and down by transformers is the voltage *between* the two transmission cables (used in $P=IV$ for the power actually delivered). The voltage *drop along* a cable, $V_{\text{drop}}=IR$, is a separate, much smaller quantity caused by the cable's own resistance — it's this drop (and the associated $I^2R$ heating) that high-voltage transmission is specifically designed to minimise.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Checking statements about high-voltage ac transmission">
Which are correct: (1) higher transmission voltage means lower current in the cables, (2) it increases efficiency, (3) it reduces heat losses, (4) it makes the cables easier to insulate, (5) more of the generated power reaches the consumer?

Power can't be created, so for the same power, a higher voltage forces a lower current — (1) is correct. Lower current means less $I^2R$ heating, so less wasted energy and higher efficiency — (2) and (3) are both correct, and consequently more power actually reaches the consumer rather than being lost as heat — (5) is correct too. Higher voltage is actually **harder**, not easier, to insulate safely, so (4) is the one incorrect statement.
</WorkedExample>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- Like poles repel, unlike poles attract; attraction alone never proves something is a magnet, only repulsion does.
- Field lines run N to S outside a magnet, never cross, and are closer together where the field is stronger.
- Soft materials (iron) magnetise/demagnetise easily; hard materials (steel) resist both — used for electromagnet cores and permanent magnets respectively.
- Induced magnetism is always attractive. Right-hand grip rule gives field direction around a current-carrying wire, coil, or solenoid.
- Motor effect: $F=BIL$ for a wire at right angles to a field; Fleming's left-hand rule (Field, Current, Motor effect) gives the direction.
- A dc motor's split-ring commutator reverses the coil current every half-turn, keeping the turning effect one-way.
- Electromagnetic induction: voltage induced when a conductor cuts field lines, or when the field through it changes. Lenz's law: the induced effect always opposes the change that caused it.
- ac generator: peak voltage ↑ with faster rotation, stronger field, larger coil, more turns; frequency = rotation frequency.
- Transformers: $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{n_p}{n_s}$; $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$. Need ac — dc induces nothing in the secondary.
- High-voltage transmission minimises $I^2R$ cable losses by keeping current low for the same transmitted power.

physics/matter.content:
## P5.1 States of matter and the particle model

Solids, liquids and gases are distinguished by three everyday properties: **fluidity** (can it flow?), **compressibility** (can you squash it into less volume?), and **typical density**.

<FormulaCard title="Macroscopic properties of the three states">
- **Solid** — rigid, effectively incompressible, high density ($10^3$–$10^4\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$).
- **Liquid** — fluid (takes the shape of the bottom of its container), effectively incompressible, high density ($\sim 10^3\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$).
- **Gas** — fluid (fills the whole container), highly compressible, low density ($\sim 1\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ at room temperature and atmospheric pressure).

Liquids and gases are together called **fluids**, since both can flow.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="A sponge isn't secretly compressible">
A sponge *looks* compressible, but the solid material it's made from isn't — it's mostly trapped air. Squeezing it pushes air out of the pockets; the solid "skeleton" itself barely changes volume. Don't let a compressible-looking object talk you out of "solids are incompressible."
</Trap>

The **particle model** explains all of this at the microscopic level: matter is made of particles in constant motion, and the *forces between them*, their *arrangement*, and their *motion* differ between the three states.

<FormulaCard title="Particle model of the three states">
| | Solid | Liquid | Gas |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forces between particles | strongly bonded to neighbours | attracted, but more weakly than in a solid | none, except during collisions |
| Arrangement | very close, fixed, often a regular lattice | very close, no regular pattern | far apart (on average), no regular pattern |
| Motion | vibrate about a fixed position | move randomly from place to place | move randomly, at high speed, in straight lines between collisions |
</FormulaCard>

A "particle" here just means the smallest unit of the substance — atom, molecule, or ion — the model doesn't care which. It predicts the same three-state behaviour regardless of what the substance actually is.

<WorkedExample title="Reading macroscopic behaviour off the particle model">
Use the particle model to explain why convection cannot occur in a solid.

Convection is the bulk movement of warmer, less dense material upwards past cooler, denser material moving down to replace it. In a solid, particles vibrate about *fixed* positions and cannot change places with each other, so there's no way for bulk regions of the material to swap positions — convection needs a fluid.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Don't project macroscopic properties onto particles">
A gas being compressible doesn't mean its particles are compressible — they're just pushed closer together. Water vapour being less dense than liquid water doesn't mean water particles are "lighter" as a gas — there are simply fewer of them per unit volume. Keep the macroscopic property (of the bulk substance) and the microscopic explanation (in terms of particles) separate.
</Trap>

## P5.2 Ideal gases and $PV = \text{constant}$

An **ideal gas** is a simplified model: identical particles in random motion, exerting no forces on each other except during collisions, taking up negligible volume, and obeying Newton's laws. Real gases near room temperature and atmospheric pressure behave close to this.

**Temperature** and **pressure** are both macroscopic properties — it's meaningless to say an individual particle "has a temperature" or "has a pressure." Instead:

<FormulaCard title="Temperature and pressure in terms of particles">
- **Temperature** reflects the *average speed* of the gas particles — higher temperature means faster particles on average.
- **Pressure** arises from particles colliding with a surface: each collision exerts a tiny force, and these average out to a force per unit area.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Heating a sealed gas">
A sealed container of gas is heated. Explain what happens to the pressure.

Pressure increases, for two combined reasons: the particles move faster on average, so (1) collisions with the walls happen more often, and (2) each collision is more forceful on average. Both effects increase the average force per unit area on the walls.
</WorkedExample>

Now hold **temperature constant** and instead shrink the container. The average particle speed doesn't change (temperature is unchanged) — but each particle now has less distance to travel between wall collisions, so collisions happen more often. Force per collision is unchanged, frequency goes up, so pressure rises.

<FormulaCard title="Boyle's law">
$$
PV = \text{constant} \qquad \text{(fixed mass of ideal gas, constant temperature)}
$$

Equivalently $P \propto \dfrac{1}{V}$ — pressure is inversely proportional to volume. For two states of the same sealed sample at the same temperature:

$$
P_1V_1 = P_2V_2
$$
</FormulaCard>

<Shortcut title="Skip the constant">
Don't bother computing the constant explicitly — just write $P_1V_1=P_2V_2$ and rearrange for whichever unknown you need, e.g. $P_1 = \dfrac{P_2V_2}{V_1}$.
</Shortcut>

<WorkedExample title="Applying P₁V₁ = P₂V₂">
A sealed gas sample has pressure $1.0\times10^5\ \text{Pa}$ and volume $60\ \text{cm}^3$. The container is compressed (no gas escapes) to $40\ \text{cm}^3$. Find the new pressure.

$$
P_2 = \frac{P_1V_1}{V_2} = \frac{(1.0\times10^5)(60)}{40} = 1.5\times10^5\ \text{Pa}
$$

Note the volumes don't need converting to $\text{m}^3$ here — as long as the *same* units are used on both sides, they cancel.
</WorkedExample>

## P5.3 State changes, latent heat, and specific latent heat

Nearly every pure substance has a fixed **melting point** (solid $\leftrightarrow$ liquid) and **boiling point** (liquid $\leftrightarrow$ gas), each at a *specific* temperature. (A few substances, like CO₂, sublime — jumping straight between solid and gas.)

<FormulaCard title="State as a function of temperature">
| Temperature | State |
|---|---|
| below melting point | solid |
| at melting point | solid/liquid |
| between melting and boiling point | liquid |
| at boiling point | liquid/gas |
| above boiling point | gas |
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Impure substances don't have a sharp melting/boiling point">
An impure substance melts and boils over a *range* of temperatures, not at a single fixed value — so you can't quote "the" melting point or boiling point for it.
</Trap>

While a substance is *changing state*, thermal energy is transferred to or from it without any change in temperature — the energy goes into pulling particles apart (melting/boiling) or is released as particles come together (freezing/condensing). Only once the whole sample has finished changing state does the temperature start moving again. This absorbed/released energy is **latent heat**: *latent heat of fusion* for melting/freezing, *latent heat of vaporisation* for boiling/condensing.

<Tip title="Temperature–energy graph shape">
Heating a solid steadily into a gas gives a graph of temperature against thermal energy transferred that rises while a single state is heating, then flattens into a plateau during each state change (melting, then boiling), before rising again.
</Tip>

<FormulaCard title="Specific latent heat">
$$
E = mL
$$

$L$ is the **specific latent heat** (J kg⁻¹) — the energy transferred per unit mass during a *complete* change of state, at constant temperature (the melting point, for fusion; the boiling point, for vaporisation).
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Latent heat of fusion">
Calculate the energy needed to change 3.0 kg of ice at 0 °C into liquid water at 0 °C. ($L_{\text{fusion, water}} = 330\ \text{kJ kg}^{-1}$.)

$$
E = mL = 3.0 \times 330\,000 = 990\,000\ \text{J} = 990\ \text{kJ}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Finding L from an experiment">
6900 kJ of thermal energy is released to the surroundings when 3.0 kg of water vapour at 100 °C condenses to liquid water at 100 °C. Find the specific latent heat of vaporisation.

$$
L = \frac{E}{m} = \frac{6\,900\,000}{3.0} = 2\,300\,000\ \text{J kg}^{-1} = 2300\ \text{kJ kg}^{-1}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Two components when temperature rises AND state changes">
If a sample is heated through a temperature rise *and* a state change, the total energy transferred is the **sum** of two separate calculations: $E=mc\Delta T$ for each temperature-rise stage (specific heat capacity $c$), plus $E=mL$ for each state-change stage. Don't try to combine them into a single formula — work out each stage on the graph separately and add the energies.
</Trap>

## P5.4 Density

<FormulaCard title="Density">
$$
\rho = \frac{m}{V}
$$

Units: $\text{kg m}^{-3}$ or $\text{g cm}^{-3}$ (equivalently g mL⁻¹ for liquids). All samples of a given substance share the same density regardless of size, so density is a way of identifying a material. An object made of several substances has an *average* density: total mass over total volume.
</FormulaCard>

<Shortcut title="Converting g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³">
Multiply by 1000: $1\ \text{g cm}^{-3} = 1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$, since $1\ \text{kg}=10^3\ \text{g}$ and $1\ \text{m}^3=10^6\ \text{cm}^3$, and $10^6/10^3=10^3$.
</Shortcut>

<WorkedExample title="Density conversion and rearranging">
Aluminium has density $2.700\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$.

(a) Convert to $\text{kg m}^{-3}$: $2.700 \times 1000 = 2700\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$.

(b) Find the volume of a 0.500 kg (= 500 g) sample:
$$
V = \frac{m}{\rho} = \frac{500}{2.700} = 185\ \text{cm}^3 \ \text{(3 s.f.)}
$$
</WorkedExample>

**Measuring density** always comes down to measuring mass (balance) and volume, but the *method* for volume depends on the sample:

<FormulaCard title="Measuring volume">
- **Regular solid** — measure dimensions with a ruler, calculate volume from the shape.
- **Irregular solid** — submerge in a partially filled measuring cylinder (or use a displacement can) and find the volume of water displaced.
- **Liquid** — pour into a measuring cylinder and read the volume scale directly; find mass by weighing the cylinder empty and then full, and subtracting.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Floating samples need a sinker">
The displacement method only works directly if the sample sinks. If it floats, tie it to a denser object of known volume (a "sinker") so the combination sinks, measure the total displaced volume, then **subtract** the sinker's own volume to isolate the sample's volume.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Density of a floating object, using a sinker">
An irregular object has mass 35.2 g and floats, so it's tied to a 447 g block of density $8.94\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$. Together they displace $105.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of water. Find the object's density.

Volume of the block: $V=\dfrac{m}{\rho}=\dfrac{447}{8.94}=50.0\ \text{cm}^3$.

Volume of the object: $105.0-50.0=55.0\ \text{cm}^3$.

Density of the object: $\rho=\dfrac{35.2}{55.0}=0.640\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$.
</WorkedExample>

<Tip title="Comparing densities across the three states">
Solids and liquids usually have *similar* densities (particles are close together in both — solids are typically only around 1.1× denser than the corresponding liquid), while gases are typically around **1000× less dense** than the liquid form, because gas particles are far apart with far fewer particles per unit volume. Water is a well-known exception where the solid (ice) is *less* dense than the liquid.
</Tip>

## P5.5 Pressure, including hydrostatic pressure

<FormulaCard title="Pressure">
$$
\text{pressure} = \frac{\text{force}}{\text{area}}, \qquad 1\ \text{N m}^{-2} = 1\ \text{Pa}
$$

Area means the area of contact over which the force acts. Increase pressure by increasing the force or shrinking the contact area; decrease it by doing the opposite.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Sharp vs wide contact areas">
Needles and knives concentrate a modest force onto a tiny area to get very high pressure (enough to cut). Snowshoes and skis spread a person's weight over a large area to get low pressure (so they don't sink). A drawing pin uses both ends of the same principle at once: same force throughout the pin, but far higher pressure at the sharp end than under your thumb.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Pressure from a distributed weight">
A table with four legs, each with a square cross-section of side 5.0 cm, has total weight 250 N. Find the pressure on the ground.

Total contact area: $4 \times (0.050)^2 = 0.010\ \text{m}^2$.

$$
\text{pressure} = \frac{250}{0.010} = 25\,000\ \text{Pa}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<FormulaCard title="Hydrostatic pressure">
$$
P = h\rho g
$$

where $h$ is depth below the surface, $\rho$ is the fluid's density, and $g$ is gravitational field strength. This depends only on depth, density, and $g$ — **not** on the shape of the container, so two points at equal depth in the same connected liquid are at equal pressure.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Where the formula comes from">
Picture a cuboid of liquid of cross-sectional area $A$ and height $h$, with its top at the liquid surface. Its volume is $Ah$, so its mass is $Ah\rho$ and its weight is $Ah\rho g$. That weight is supported by the pressure acting over the base area $A$, so pressure at depth $h$ is $\dfrac{Ah\rho g}{A}=h\rho g$.
</Tip>

<Trap title="Total pressure vs pressure due to the fluid alone">
The pressure measured at a depth in a liquid (or under an object) is the **sum** of the hydrostatic pressure from the fluid/object and any pressure already present above it (typically atmospheric pressure). "The pressure due to the water" specifically excludes the atmospheric contribution — subtract it off before applying $P=h\rho g$.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Finding depth from total pressure">
At a point on the sea floor, total pressure is $3.16\times10^6\ \text{Pa}$. Seawater density is $1020\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$, atmospheric pressure is $1.0\times10^5\ \text{Pa}$, and $g=10\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$. Find the depth.

Pressure due to the water alone:
$$
3.16\times10^6 - 1.0\times10^5 = 3.06\times10^6\ \text{Pa}
$$

Rearranging $P=h\rho g$:
$$
h = \frac{P}{\rho g} = \frac{3.06\times10^6}{1020\times10} = 300\ \text{m}
$$
</WorkedExample>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- Solids: rigid, incompressible, dense. Liquids: fluid, incompressible, dense. Gases: fluid, compressible, low density. Explain all of it via particle forces/arrangement/motion.
- Ideal gas at constant temperature: $PV=\text{constant}$, so $P_1V_1=P_2V_2$ — skip computing the constant explicitly.
- Temperature $\leftrightarrow$ average particle speed; pressure $\leftrightarrow$ frequency and force of particle collisions with a surface.
- State changes happen at constant temperature (melting/boiling point); latent heat $E=mL$. If temperature also changes, add the $mc\Delta T$ stages separately.
- Density $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$; $1\ \text{g cm}^{-3}=1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$. For irregular or floating solids, use displacement (with a sinker if it floats).
- Pressure $=\dfrac{\text{force}}{\text{area}}$. Hydrostatic pressure $P=h\rho g$, independent of container shape; add atmospheric pressure for the total, or subtract it to isolate "pressure due to the fluid."

physics/mechanics.title: Mechanics
physics/mechanics.content:
## P3.1 Scalars and vectors

<FormulaCard title="Scalar vs vector">
A **scalar** has magnitude only (mass, time, energy, temperature, speed, distance). A **vector** has magnitude *and* direction (force, velocity, acceleration, displacement, momentum).
</FormulaCard>

A scalar can still be negative (a temperature, a change in mass) — "scalar" just means direction plays no role in how the quantity is defined. A vector's sign only makes sense once you've fixed which direction counts as positive; that choice is always arbitrary, but must stay consistent throughout a calculation.

<Tip title="Distance vs displacement, speed vs velocity">
Distance and speed are the scalar versions — magnitude only, no direction. Displacement and velocity are the vector versions — distance/speed *in a particular direction*. So distance is the magnitude of displacement, and speed is the magnitude of velocity, but only when the motion doesn't change direction along the way (otherwise distance keeps accumulating while displacement can shrink, cancel, or reverse sign).
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Picking out distance vs displacement">
A car laps a circular track (circumference 630 m, radius 100 m) starting at S. Halfway round, at point H, it has covered 315 m — but its displacement from S is only +200 m (the straight-line gap). Back at S, distance travelled is 630 m, but displacement from S is zero.

The lesson: **distance never decreases** — it just keeps adding up. **Displacement** only cares about the straight-line gap between start and current position, so it can shrink, hit zero, or go negative even while distance climbs steadily.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Only components in the direction asked matter">
"A person walks 5 m north, 6 m east, 7 m south, 8 m west — what's the displacement north of the start?" Ignore the east/west legs entirely; they don't affect north–south displacement. Net north–south movement is $5-7=-2\,\text{m}$, i.e. 2 m *south* of the start. Always resolve a multi-leg journey into the one axis the question actually asks about before doing anything else.
</Trap>

## P3.2 Speed, velocity, and acceleration

<FormulaCard title="Speed, velocity, acceleration">
$$
\text{speed} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}, \qquad \text{velocity} = \frac{\text{change in displacement}}{\text{time}}, \qquad \text{acceleration} = \frac{\text{change in velocity}}{\text{time}}
$$

These only apply directly when the relevant quantity (speed/velocity, or acceleration) is **constant** over the interval considered.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Constant speed doesn't mean zero acceleration">
An object moving at constant *speed* around a curve is still accelerating, because its *velocity* (direction included) is changing. Acceleration is about velocity, not speed — and an object can accelerate from an instant of zero velocity too (a ball at the top of a bounce has zero velocity but nonzero acceleration).
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Change in velocity when direction reverses">
A ball hits a bat at 25 m/s and rebounds at 20 m/s in the opposite direction, over 0.30 s. Taking the incoming direction as positive, find the acceleration.

$$
u = +25, \quad v = -20 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Delta v = -20-25 = -45\ \text{m s}^{-1}
$$

$$
a = \frac{\Delta v}{t} = \frac{-45}{0.30} = -150\ \text{m s}^{-2}
$$

The minus sign just means the acceleration points opposite to the ball's original direction — entirely expected, since the bat reverses its motion.
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Set up a sign convention once, then stick to it">
Before touching any numbers, pick which direction is positive and write down $u$, $v$, $s$, $a$ with the correct sign for *that* choice. Almost every kinematics slip comes from switching sign convention halfway through, not from the arithmetic itself.
</Shortcut>

## P3.3 Motion graphs: gradients and areas

<FormulaCard title="What the gradient means">
Gradient of **distance–time** = speed. Gradient of **displacement–time** = velocity. Gradient of **velocity–time** = acceleration.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="What the area means">
Area under **speed–time** graph = distance moved. Area under **velocity–time** graph = change in displacement (area *below* the axis counts as negative displacement).
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Distance–time graphs can never slope downwards">
Distance is a scalar that only ever accumulates, so a genuine distance–time graph never has a negative gradient. A graph that dips downward as an object returns to its start is a **displacement**–time graph, mislabelled — watch for this exact mislabelling trap in questions.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Reading a velocity–time graph for a bouncing ball">
A ball is released, falls, and bounces repeatedly; the graph takes the downward direction as positive. Between bounces the velocity rises from a large positive (downward) value at impact to a large negative (upward) value just after, then decreases in magnitude (upward, decelerating) until it hits zero at the top of the bounce, then increases again (downward, accelerating) into the next bounce.

The ball is at the **top of a bounce** exactly when velocity crosses zero while changing from negative (upward) to positive (downward) — that's the only moment its direction of motion actually reverses.
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Split areas into signed triangles/rectangles">
For a velocity–time graph made of straight segments, compute the area of each triangle or trapezium separately, keeping the sign (positive above the axis, negative below), then add them. This handles "net displacement" questions cleanly even when the object changes direction several times.
</Shortcut>

## P3.4 Average speed, velocity, and acceleration

<FormulaCard title="Averages over a whole journey">
$$
\text{average speed} = \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}, \qquad \text{average velocity} = \frac{\text{net change in displacement}}{\text{total time}}, \qquad \text{average acceleration} = \frac{\text{net change in velocity}}{\text{total time}}
$$
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Don't average the speeds — average the journey">
If an object covers 30 m in 30 s then 70 m in the next 20 s, the average speed is **not** the mean of $1.0$ and $3.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (which would ignore how long each speed lasted). It's total distance over total time: $\dfrac{100}{50}=2.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Average acceleration can be zero even with plenty of acceleration in between">
An object starts and finishes at rest (velocity zero at $t=0$ and at $t=60\,\text{s}$), speeding up and slowing down repeatedly in between. Net change in velocity $=0-0=0$, so average acceleration $=0/60=0$ — even though the object was clearly accelerating (positively and negatively) throughout the 60 s.
</WorkedExample>

## P3.5 Equations of uniform motion

<FormulaCard title="The three suvat-style equations (constant acceleration)">
$$
v = u+at, \qquad s = \tfrac12(u+v)t, \qquad v^2-u^2 = 2as
$$

$u$ = initial velocity, $v$ = final velocity, $a$ = (constant) acceleration, $t$ = time, $s$ = displacement.
</FormulaCard>

<Shortcut title="Pick the equation that skips the unknown you don't have">
$v^2-u^2=2as$ is the one that avoids $t$ entirely — reach for it whenever a question gives you $u$, $a$, and $s$ (or asks for one of them) but says nothing about time.
</Shortcut>

<WorkedExample title="Using v² − u² = 2as when time isn't given">
A stone is thrown upward at 5.0 m/s from a 30 m cliff, with downward acceleration 10 m/s² throughout. Find its speed hitting the sea (taking downwards as positive).

$$
u=-5.0,\quad s=+30,\quad a=+10
$$

$$
v^2 = u^2+2as = (-5.0)^2+2(10)(30) = 25+600=625 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v=25\ \text{m s}^{-1}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Squaring erases the sign of u — but check it makes physical sense">
$u^2$ is the same whether $u$ is $+5$ or $-5$, which is exactly why $v^2-u^2=2as$ works regardless of which way the object was initially moving. But when you take the square root to find $v$, only the positive root usually makes physical sense (speed is never negative) — think about the actual direction of travel before quoting a signed velocity from this equation.
</Trap>

## P3.6 Types of force

<FormulaCard title="Contact and non-contact forces">
**Non-contact** (act through a field, no touching needed): weight (gravitational), magnetic, electrostatic. **Contact** (need the objects touching): normal contact, drag (incl. air resistance), friction, upthrust, thrust, lift, tension.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Never call the normal contact force 'reaction'">
Calling normal contact force "reaction" invites the classic error of pairing it with weight as a "Newton's third law pair" — they are not (see P3.9). Always name it the **normal contact force**.
</Trap>

<Tip title="Drag and friction are both resistive, but from different causes">
Drag (most commonly air resistance) opposes motion through a *fluid* (liquid or gas); friction opposes *sliding between two solids* in contact. Both act opposite to the relevant relative motion, and are sometimes lumped together as "total resistive forces."
</Tip>

## P3.7 Force diagrams and resultant force

Every force arrow starts on the object it acts on, points in the force's direction, and is labelled with its type, its size, and what's exerting it. **Resultant force is never drawn as its own arrow** — it's the combined effect of all the real forces already on the diagram, not an extra force in its own right.

<FormulaCard title="Resultant force in one dimension">
Resultant force = (total force one way) − (total force the opposite way), acting in the direction of whichever total is larger. If the two totals are equal, the resultant is zero and the forces are **balanced**.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Resolving into perpendicular directions separately">
A plane in flight: thrust 200 kN forward, drag 140 kN backward, weight 160 kN down, lift 160 kN up.

Horizontally: $200-140=60\,\text{kN}$ forward. Vertically: $160-160=0$ — balanced. The overall resultant here is just the horizontal 60 kN forward, because the vertical forces happen to cancel exactly.
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Work out an unknown force from 'resultant = zero'">
If a question states (or implies via constant velocity) that the resultant force is zero, every unknown force is just found by making the two opposing totals equal — no need to solve simultaneous equations. E.g. a submerged rock with resultant force zero, weight 4000 N down, upthrust 1500 N up: the normal contact force must supply the remaining $4000-1500=2500\,\text{N}$ up.
</Shortcut>

## P3.8 Force and extension (Hooke's law)

<FormulaCard title="Hooke's law">
$$
F = kx
$$

Within the limit of proportionality, extension $x$ is proportional to tension force $F$; the constant $k$ is the **spring constant** (units $\text{N m}^{-1}$) — force needed per unit extension. The gradient of a force–extension graph *is* $k$.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Elastic limit vs limit of proportionality — related, not identical">
Beyond the **limit of proportionality**, $F=kx$ stops holding (the graph curves). Beyond the **elastic limit**, the material no longer returns to its original length once unloaded (permanent, "plastic" deformation). These two points often coincide, but the question is testing whether you know they're conceptually distinct facts about the graph, not the same fact stated twice.
</Tip>

<FormulaCard title="Elastic potential energy">
$$
E = \tfrac12 Fx = \tfrac12 kx^2
$$

This is the area under the force–extension graph — valid as *recoverable* stored energy only while the elastic limit hasn't been exceeded.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Stretch beyond the elastic limit, and not all the work done is recoverable">
If a wire is stretched past its elastic limit, the *total* work done (full area under the loading curve) is more than the energy you get back on unloading. Only the recoverable part (area of the triangle traced out during unloading) counts as stored elastic potential energy; the rest is dissipated as heat during the permanent extension.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Extension and stored energy for a loaded spring">
A spring, $k=25\ \text{N m}^{-1}$, supports a 0.30 kg mass. Find its extension and the energy stored.

$$
x = \frac{F}{k} = \frac{mg}{k} = \frac{0.30\times10}{25} = 0.12\ \text{m}
$$

$$
E = \tfrac12 kx^2 = \tfrac12(25)(0.12)^2 = 0.18\ \text{J}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Combining identical springs">
$n$ identical springs (constant $k$) **in series**: same force stretches the combination $n$ times as far, so combined constant is $k/n$. **In parallel**: $n$ times the force is needed for the same extension, so combined constant is $nk$ — the opposite pattern to resistors in series/parallel.
</Shortcut>

## P3.9 Newton's three laws

<FormulaCard title="Newton's first law">
A body stays at rest, or moves at constant velocity in a straight line, unless a **resultant** external force acts on it. Constant velocity ⇔ zero resultant force — not "a force is needed to keep something moving."
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="A force being present doesn't mean it's the resultant">
A cruising aircraft needs thrust to balance drag, but thrust is not *the* resultant force — the resultant is zero, because thrust and drag cancel. Don't confuse "a force acts to maintain motion against resistance" with "there is a nonzero resultant force causing that motion" — the two statements are opposites.
</Trap>

<FormulaCard title="Newton's second law">
$$
F = ma
$$

Here $F$ **must** be the resultant force. The resulting acceleration is in the same direction as the resultant. (More generally, $F$ = rate of change of momentum; $F=ma$ is the special case where mass stays constant.)
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Finding acceleration from a force diagram">
A 1200 kg car has a 3200 N driving force and an 800 N resistive force, both horizontal. Find its acceleration.

$$
F_{\text{resultant}} = 3200-800 = 2400\ \text{N} \qquad a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{2400}{1200} = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}
$$

This doesn't tell you whether the car is speeding up moving forward or slowing down moving backward — only the magnitude and direction of the *acceleration*, not the velocity.
</WorkedExample>

<FormulaCard title="Newton's third law">
If body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts an equal, opposite force **of the same type** on A. The pair always acts on **two different objects**.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Weight and normal contact force are never a Newton's third law pair">
They're equal and opposite *when an object isn't accelerating* — but that equality is a consequence of Newton's **first** law (zero resultant force), not the third. A genuine Newton-third pair must be the *same type* of force (both normal contact, or both gravitational, etc.) and must act on *two different bodies* — e.g. the normal contact force the floor exerts on you, and the normal contact force you exert on the floor. Weight (gravitational, exerted by the Earth) and normal contact force (exerted by the floor) are different types acting on the *same* body, so they fail on both counts. Avoid the words "action" and "reaction" entirely — they invite exactly this mix-up.
</Trap>

## P3.10 Mass, weight, and gravitational field strength

<FormulaCard title="Mass vs weight">
**Mass** is the amount of matter (inertia) — a scalar, unchanged wherever the object is. **Weight** is the gravitational *force* on that mass — a vector, and it changes with location.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="Weight from mass and field strength">
$$
W = mg
$$

$g$ is gravitational field strength (force per unit mass), $\approx 10\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$ on Earth. On the Moon $g\approx1.6\,\text{N kg}^{-1}$; on Jupiter $\approx26\,\text{N kg}^{-1}$.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="A 1 kg mass does not 'equal' 10 N">
$W=mg$ relates two *different* quantities via a constant — it's exactly like saying a car at 10 m/s covers 10 m in 1 s: that doesn't mean "1 s equals 10 m." A 1 kg mass weighs 10 N on Earth, but the same 1 kg mass weighs only 1.6 N on the Moon — the mass hasn't changed, only the weight has, because $g$ is different.
</Trap>

<FormulaCard title="Free-fall acceleration">
With only weight acting, $F_{\text{resultant}}=mg$, so $a=F/m=g$. A freely-falling object accelerates at exactly $g$, regardless of its mass — heavier and lighter objects (in the absence of air resistance) fall together.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="'Weightless' astronauts still have weight">
Orbiting astronauts feel weightless because they and their spacecraft are both in free fall, accelerating at $g$ together — so there's no normal contact force between them to feel. This is **apparent** weightlessness, not true weightlessness: their weight is still what's causing the fall. True weightlessness only occurs with zero gravitational field, i.e. deep space.
</Trap>

<FormulaCard title="Terminal velocity">
Falling through air, weight (constant) acts down and air resistance (increasing with speed) acts up. Acceleration starts at $g$ and shrinks as speed builds, until air resistance equals weight — resultant force and acceleration both hit zero, and the object has reached **terminal velocity**.
</FormulaCard>

<Shortcut title="A shape change resets the terminal velocity">
Increasing effective cross-sectional area (e.g. opening a parachute) increases air resistance at a given speed, so a *lower* speed is now enough to balance the weight — the object decelerates from its old (higher) terminal velocity down to a new, lower one. While decelerating, air resistance briefly exceeds weight, giving a resultant force opposing motion (i.e. upward, for something falling).
</Shortcut>

## P3.11 Momentum

<FormulaCard title="Momentum">
$$
p = mv
$$

Vector, in the same direction as velocity. Units: $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$, equivalently N s.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Combine momenta as vectors, not magnitudes">
Two objects with momenta $0.50\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ right and $0.80\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ left don't add to $1.3$; taking left as negative, the total is $0.50-0.80=-0.30\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$, i.e. $0.30\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ **left**. Always fix a sign convention before adding momenta.
</Trap>

<FormulaCard title="Conservation of momentum">
In a closed system (no external forces), total momentum before an interaction = total momentum after. Momentum is conserved separately in **every** direction.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Conservation of momentum on an ice rink">
A 70 kg adult and 35 kg child, both stationary, push apart; the child slides off at 0.80 m/s. Find the adult's speed.

Total momentum starts and stays at zero, so the two final momenta are equal and opposite:

$$
70v = 35\times0.80 = 28\ \text{kg m s}^{-1} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = 0.40\ \text{m s}^{-1}
$$

directed opposite to the child's motion.
</WorkedExample>

<FormulaCard title="Force as rate of change of momentum">
$$
F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}
$$

Equivalent to $F=ma$ when mass is constant; this is the more fundamental statement of Newton's second law.
</FormulaCard>

<Shortcut title="Bending your knees on landing — spread the same Δp over more time">
The change in momentum on landing is fixed by how far you fell (it doesn't depend on landing technique). Bending your knees increases the *time* over which that momentum change happens, which — since $F=\Delta p/\Delta t$ — directly reduces the force (and hence the acceleration) your body experiences. Same logic covers airbags, crumple zones, and catching a ball with a "give" in your arm.
</Shortcut>

## P3.12 Work, energy, and power

<FormulaCard title="Work done by a force">
$$
W = Fs
$$

$s$ is the distance moved **in the direction of the force**. If the force acts at angle $\theta$ to the direction of motion, use $W=Fs\cos\theta$.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Work is energy transfer, and it's a two-way street">
When a force does positive work on an object, the object's energy increases by that amount; when the object does work against a force (moves against it), its energy decreases by that amount. By Newton's third law, if A does work $W$ on B, B's reaction does work $-W$ on A — energy is transferred, not created, exactly as conservation of energy requires.
</Tip>

<FormulaCard title="Gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy">
$$
\Delta E_p = mgh, \qquad E_k = \tfrac12 mv^2
$$

$h$ is a *difference* in height — potential energy has no absolute zero; only differences matter, and you're free to choose the reference height that's most convenient for a given problem.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Splitting work done against friction from work done against gravity">
A 500 kg trunk is pulled 4.0 m up a ramp by a 2000 N force, rising 1.2 m vertically. Find the work done against friction.

$$
W_{\text{applied}} = Fs = 2000\times4.0 = 8000\ \text{J}, \qquad \Delta E_p = mgh = 500\times10\times1.2 = 6000\ \text{J}
$$

$$
W_{\text{friction}} = 8000-6000 = 2000\ \text{J}
$$

The applied force's work either raises the trunk (gravitational PE) or is lost to friction — nothing else is happening, so the two must add up to the total.
</WorkedExample>

<FormulaCard title="Power">
$$
P = \frac{W}{t} = \frac{E}{t}
$$

Rate of doing work / transferring energy, in watts ($1\,\text{W}=1\,\text{J s}^{-1}$).
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Power from a change in kinetic energy">
A 1200 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 8.0 s. Find the useful output power.

$$
\Delta E_k = \tfrac12(1200)(20)^2 = 240\,000\ \text{J} \qquad P = \frac{E}{t} = \frac{240\,000}{8.0} = 30\,000\ \text{W}
$$

The engine's actual power output is higher than this, since it's never 100% efficient.
</WorkedExample>

<FormulaCard title="Efficiency">
$$
\%\ \text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output (energy or power)}}{\text{total input (energy or power)}}\times100
$$

Never reaches 100% in practice; "useful" and "wasted" are defined relative to the *purpose* of the device, not by any absolute judgement about the form of energy.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="The same energy form can be useful in one device and wasted in another">
Light is useful output from a lamp but wasted output from a heater; heat is useful output from a heater but wasted output from a lamp. Always check what the device is *for* before labelling an energy output as useful or wasted.
</Tip>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- Distance/speed are scalars (magnitude only); displacement/velocity/acceleration/force/momentum are vectors (need a sign convention, fixed once and kept consistent).
- Gradient: distance–time → speed; displacement–time → velocity; velocity–time → acceleration. Area under velocity–time → change in displacement (signed).
- $v=u+at$, $s=\tfrac12(u+v)t$, $v^2-u^2=2as$ — pick whichever skips the variable you don't have.
- Resultant force = vector sum of all real forces; never draw it as an extra force. $F=ma$ uses the resultant only.
- Newton 1: zero resultant ⇔ constant velocity. Newton 3: equal, opposite, same type, different objects — never weight-vs-normal-contact.
- $F=kx$ and $E=\tfrac12kx^2=\tfrac12Fx$ up to the elastic limit; series springs soften ($k/n$), parallel springs stiffen ($nk$).
- $W=mg$; free fall acceleration $=g$ regardless of mass; terminal velocity is where air resistance balances weight.
- $p=mv$ (vector); momentum conserved in a closed system, direction by direction; $F=\Delta p/\Delta t$.
- $W=Fs$ (or $Fs\cos\theta$); $\Delta E_p=mgh$; $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$; $P=E/t$; efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{useful}}{\text{total input}}\times100\%$.
