physics/radioactivity.title: Radioactivity
physics/radioactivity.content:
## P7.1 The nuclear model of the atom

<FormulaCard title="The nuclear model">
An atom has a tiny, dense **nucleus** at its centre, containing one or more **protons** and (except for the most common hydrogen nucleus) one or more **neutrons** — collectively, **nucleons**. Outside the nucleus is mostly empty space, occupied by one or more orbiting **electrons**.
</FormulaCard>

The scale here is easy to underestimate: a nucleus is typically around 100,000 times smaller in radius than the whole atom, yet holds over 99.9% of its mass. Almost all of an atom's volume — and its overall size — comes from the electrons' orbits, not from the (comparatively minuscule) nucleus.

<WorkedExample title="Finding neutrons from protons and nucleon count">
A gold atom has 79 protons and 197 nucleons in total. How many neutrons does it have?

Nucleons = protons + neutrons, so neutrons $= 197-79 = 118$.
</WorkedExample>

## P7.2 Relative charges and masses of subatomic particles

<FormulaCard title="Charges and masses">
| Particle | Relative mass | Relative charge |
|---|---|---|
| Proton | 1 | $+1$ |
| Neutron | 1 | $0$ |
| Electron | $\approx\frac{1}{2000}$ | $-1$ |

A proton and an electron carry exactly equal and opposite charge, despite the proton being roughly 2000 times heavier. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so its charges cancel exactly.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="What actually holds a nucleus together">
Protons are all positively charged, so packed together in a tiny nucleus they should repel each other strongly — and they would, if electrostatic repulsion were the only force at play. What actually holds the nucleus together is the **strong nuclear force**, a short-range attractive force between nucleons that overpowers the electrostatic repulsion at nuclear distances.
</Tip>

## P7.3 Atomic number and mass number

<FormulaCard title="Atomic number and mass number">
**Atomic number** ($Z$, also "proton number") = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom. It determines which element the atom is. **Mass number** ($A$, also "nucleon number") = total protons + neutrons.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Working backwards from partial information">
An atom has 19 nucleons and 10 neutrons. How many electrons does it have?

Protons $=$ nucleons $-$ neutrons $=19-10=9$. A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons, so it also has **9 electrons**.
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Atomic and mass numbers from different starting facts">
Find the atomic number and mass number of: (a) an atom with 1 proton and 0 neutrons; (b) an atom with 16 neutrons and 15 electrons; (c) an atom with 195 nucleons and 117 neutrons.

(a) Atomic number $=1$; mass number $=1+0=1$.

(b) Electrons $=$ protons, so atomic number $=15$; mass number $=15+16=31$.

(c) Protons $=195-117=78$, so atomic number $=78$; mass number (nucleon count) $=195$.
</WorkedExample>

## P7.4 Isotopes

<FormulaCard title="Isotopes">
**Isotopes** are nuclides of the same element — same atomic number (same number of protons) but different numbers of neutrons, and hence different mass numbers.
</FormulaCard>

Every element has at least a few known isotopes — some have thirty or more — though for most elements only one or two of these are naturally stable in significant quantities.

<WorkedExample title="Deciding whether nuclides must be the same element">
Which of these must be isotopes of the same element? (1) 19 protons, 20 neutrons. (2) 20 protons, 20 neutrons. (3) 19 protons, 19 neutrons. (4) 40 nucleons (total unspecified split).

Isotopes of the same element share the same **atomic number**, i.e. the same proton count. Nuclides (1) and (3) both have 19 protons, so they **must** be isotopes of the same element. Nuclide (2) has 20 protons — a different element from (1) and (3). Nuclide (4) only gives a nucleon total, not a proton count, so it could have 19 protons (matching (1) and (3)), 20 (matching (2)), or any other split — there isn't enough information to pin it down.
</WorkedExample>

## P7.5 Nuclide notation

<FormulaCard title="Nuclide notation">
$$
{}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}
$$

$X$ is the element symbol, $A$ (top) is the mass number, $Z$ (bottom) is the atomic number. Number of neutrons $=A-Z$. The same nuclide is often written more compactly as, e.g., "He-4" or "U-238" — just the symbol and mass number, with no direct information about the proton count on its own.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Reading protons and neutrons off nuclide notation">
Find the protons and neutrons in ${}^{1}_{1}\text{H}$, ${}^{107}_{47}\text{Ag}$, and ${}^{238}_{92}\text{U}$.

Protons = atomic number (bottom), neutrons = mass number $-$ atomic number:

$$
{}^{1}_{1}\text{H}:\ 1\ \text{proton},\ 1-1=0\ \text{neutrons}
$$
$$
{}^{107}_{47}\text{Ag}:\ 47\ \text{protons},\ 107-47=60\ \text{neutrons}
$$
$$
{}^{238}_{92}\text{U}:\ 92\ \text{protons},\ 238-92=146\ \text{neutrons}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Writing nuclide notation from a description">
Write nuclide notation for: (a) phosphorus with 15 protons, 17 neutrons; (b) barium with 82 neutrons, 138 nucleons; (c) Ra-226 with 138 neutrons.

(a) Atomic number $=15$, mass number $=15+17=32$: ${}^{32}_{15}\text{P}$.

(b) Protons $=138-82=56$: ${}^{138}_{56}\text{Ba}$.

(c) Protons $=226-138=88$: ${}^{226}_{88}\text{Ra}$.
</WorkedExample>

## P7.6 Ionisation of atoms

<FormulaCard title="Ionisation">
An atom that **gains or loses electrons** becomes charged — it's now an **ion**, not an atom. Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, giving a **positive** ion; gaining electrons gives a **negative** ion. Crucially, ionisation never changes the number of protons or neutrons — only electrons move.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Ionisation never touches the nucleus">
Whatever causes the ionisation — friction, ionic bonding, or ionising radiation — only electrons are gained or lost. The atomic number and mass number of the nucleus stay exactly the same; only the charge (and hence the electron count) changes.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Finding the composition of an ion, then its neutral atom">
An ion has 45 nucleons, 19 electrons, and a charge of $+2$. It then gains electrons to become a neutral atom. Find the protons, neutrons, and electrons of the resulting atom.

A charge of $+2$ means 2 more protons than electrons: protons $=19+2=21$. Neutrons $=45-21=24$. As a neutral atom, electrons $=$ protons $=21$.
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Ionisation doesn't change atomic or mass number">
An atom of ${}^{58}_{28}\text{Ni}$ gains two electrons. What are the atomic number and mass number of the resulting ion?

Gaining electrons only changes the electron count, not the nucleus. Atomic number stays **28**, mass number stays **58** — the ion is just $\text{Ni}^{2-}$.
</WorkedExample>

## P7.7 Unstable nuclei and radioactive decay

<FormulaCard title="Radioactive decay">
Some nuclides are **stable** and persist indefinitely; others are **unstable** and eventually **decay**, emitting radiation (alpha, beta, and/or gamma) as they do so. A nuclide that decays is described as **radioactive**.
</FormulaCard>

An unstable nucleus might decay straight into a stable one and stop there, or it might decay into another unstable nuclide, continuing through a **decay chain** — possibly mixing different types of emission — until a stable nuclide is finally reached.

## P7.8 The random nature of decay

<Tip title="Random doesn't mean unpredictable in every sense">
It's impossible to say *when* any individual unstable nucleus will decay — there's no known trigger, and the process is genuinely **spontaneous**. But it *is* possible to measure the **probability** that a nucleus of a given type decays in a given time period, which is exactly what half-life captures (see below). Think of it like rolling a die repeatedly: you can't predict which roll gives the first six, but you can state the probability of a six on any given roll is $\frac16$.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Checking claims about decay">
True or false: (1) heating a radioactive substance makes it decay faster; (2) an unstable nucleus can decay into another unstable nucleus; (3) an element's isotopes are either all stable or all unstable.

(1) **False** — unlike chemical reaction rates, nuclear decay rate is completely unaffected by temperature (or any other external condition anyone has found). (2) **True** — this is exactly what happens in a decay chain. (3) **False** — most elements have a mix of stable and unstable isotopes.
</WorkedExample>

## P7.9 Alpha, beta, and gamma: nature and properties

<FormulaCard title="Alpha, beta, gamma at a glance">
| | Alpha ($\alpha$) | Beta ($\beta^-$) | Gamma ($\gamma$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nature | 2 protons + 2 neutrons (a He nucleus) | a fast electron | electromagnetic radiation |
| Notation | ${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ | ${}^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$ | — |
| Mass | 4 (proton masses) | $\approx\frac{1}{2000}$ | 0 |
| Charge | $+2$ | $-1$ | $0$ |
| Typical speed | $\approx0.1c$ | $\approx0.8c$ | $c$ |
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Why beta's nuclide notation has atomic number −1">
A beta particle's "atomic number" of $-1$ isn't literal (it isn't an antiproton) — it's a bookkeeping trick so charge balances correctly in decay equations, since an electron's charge is the negative of a proton's. Its mass number of 0 is likewise just a statement that its mass is negligible next to a nucleon's.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Matching properties to radiation type">
Which type of radiation: is negatively charged? has the greatest mass? is a form of electromagnetic radiation? travels fastest? consists of two protons and two neutrons?

Negatively charged — **beta**. Greatest mass — **alpha**. Electromagnetic — **gamma**. Fastest — **gamma** (travels at $c$). Two protons and two neutrons — **alpha**.
</WorkedExample>

## P7.10 Nuclear (decay) equations

<FormulaCard title="What each decay does to the nucleus">
**Alpha decay**: nucleus ejects 2 protons + 2 neutrons as a single particle. Atomic number $-2$, mass number $-4$. **Beta decay**: a neutron converts into a proton (which stays) plus an emitted electron. Atomic number $+1$, mass number unchanged. **Gamma decay**: only excess energy is released — no change to atomic number or mass number.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="Conservation in decay equations">
$$
{}^{A}_{Z}\text{X} \rightarrow {}^{A-4}_{Z-2}\text{Y} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} \qquad\text{(alpha)}
$$
$$
{}^{A}_{Z}\text{X} \rightarrow {}^{A}_{Z+1}\text{Y} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e} \qquad\text{(beta)}
$$

Mass numbers must balance across the arrow (no nucleons created or destroyed), and atomic numbers must balance too (charge conserved) — use these two checks to find any missing value in an equation.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Completing an alpha decay equation">
Thorium-232 undergoes alpha decay to become an isotope of radium (atomic number 88). Complete the decay equation.

Mass number: $232-4=228$. As a check, thorium's atomic number must be $88+2=90$ (radium's 88 plus the alpha particle's 2), which is correct for thorium.

$$
{}^{232}_{90}\text{Th} \rightarrow {}^{228}_{88}\text{Ra} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Following on with a beta decay">
The radium-228 produced above undergoes beta decay to become an isotope of actinium (Ac). Write the decay equation.

Beta decay leaves the mass number unchanged (228) and increases the atomic number by 1 ($88\rightarrow89$):

$$
{}^{228}_{88}\text{Ra} \rightarrow {}^{228}_{89}\text{Ac} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e}
$$

Check: mass numbers $228=228+0$; atomic numbers $88=89+(-1)$. Both balance.
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Tracking a nuclide through a sequence of decays">
Starting from ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$, find the resulting nuclide after: (a) one beta decay; (b) one alpha decay then one gamma decay; (c) one alpha decay and two beta decays.

(a) Beta leaves $A$ unchanged, $Z\rightarrow Z+1$: ${}^{A}_{Z+1}\text{Y}$.

(b) Alpha: $A\rightarrow A-4$, $Z\rightarrow Z-2$. Gamma changes neither. Result: ${}^{A-4}_{Z-2}\text{Y}$.

(c) Alpha changes $A$ by $-4$, $Z$ by $-2$; each beta changes $A$ by $0$, $Z$ by $+1$. Net over one alpha and two betas: $A\rightarrow A-4$, $Z\rightarrow Z-2+1+1=Z$. Result: ${}^{A-4}_{Z}\text{Y}$ — same element as the original, since the atomic number ends up unchanged.
</WorkedExample>

## P7.11 Penetrating power of alpha, beta, and gamma

<FormulaCard title="Penetrating ability">
**Alpha**: blocked by paper or skin; travels only a few cm in air. **Beta**: blocked by thin metal, usually passes through skin; travels up to several metres in air. **Gamma**: needs several cm of dense material (e.g. lead) to significantly reduce it; travels up to hundreds of metres in air.
</FormulaCard>

<Shortcut title="Identifying a source's emissions by what stops it">
Place absorbers of increasing thickness/density between a source and a counter and watch the count rate. Paper removes only alpha's contribution; thin aluminium additionally removes beta; thick lead is needed to remove most of gamma. Whatever count rate remains after each barrier tells you which type(s) are still getting through.
</Shortcut>

<WorkedExample title="Identifying emission types from absorber tests">
A counter reads a high count rate near a source. Paper barely changes the reading; thin aluminium reduces it significantly but it stays well above the reading with no source present. What is the source most likely emitting?

Paper having no real effect rules out **alpha** (paper would block it). Aluminium reducing the count significantly, but not to background level, indicates **beta** is present (blocked by aluminium) alongside **gamma** (aluminium can't stop it, and there's still a clear excess above background).
</WorkedExample>

## P7.12 Ionising power, and deflection in fields

<FormulaCard title="Ionising ability, and the trade-off with penetration">
**Alpha is the most ionising, gamma the least**, with beta in between — the exact opposite order to penetrating power. A particle that interacts strongly with matter (highly ionising) loses its energy quickly and doesn't get far; one that barely interacts (weakly ionising) travels much further before losing energy — that's why penetration and ionising ability trade off against each other.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="Deflection in electric and magnetic fields">
Charged particles (alpha, beta) are deflected by both electric and magnetic fields; gamma rays, being uncharged, are deflected by **neither**. Alpha and beta deflect in **opposite** directions (opposite charge signs). Beta deflects **more** than alpha for the same field, mainly because beta particles are so much lighter — despite alpha having twice the charge, its far greater mass (roughly 8000× beta's) dominates the acceleration $a=F/m$, and its lower speed only partly compensates.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Identifying three radiation types from field and ionisation clues">
Three radiation types P, Q, R: in a magnetic field, P and R deflect in opposite directions while Q isn't deflected at all; R is the most ionising of the three. Identify P, Q, and R.

No deflection means uncharged, so Q is **gamma**. P and R deflect oppositely, so they're **alpha** and **beta** (opposite charges) — and since alpha is the most ionising of the three, R is **alpha** and P is **beta**.
</WorkedExample>

## P7.13 Background radiation

<FormulaCard title="Sources of background radiation">
Background radiation is always present at a low level, mostly **natural** (over 80% — radon gas, rocks and buildings, cosmic rays, food and drink) with a smaller **artificial** share (under 20% — the vast majority of that from medical procedures, with a small remainder from nuclear power and weapons testing).
</FormulaCard>

<Shortcut title="Always correct measured count rates for background">
$$
\text{source count rate} = \text{count rate with source present} - \text{mean background count rate}
$$

Measure the background rate with the source removed (but detector left in place) and subtract it before doing any half-life or count-rate calculation involving the source.
</Shortcut>

<WorkedExample title="Correcting a measurement for background radiation">
A source gives a measured count rate of 200 cps. With the source removed (detector unmoved), the reading is 10 cps. Explain the non-zero reading, find the true source count rate, and give one reason background radiation might be higher in one region than another.

The non-zero reading with no source present is **background radiation** — low-level ionising radiation always present in the environment, mainly from natural sources like rocks and cosmic rays. True source count rate $=200-10=190\ \text{cps}$. Background can vary regionally because, for example, different rock and soil types contain different concentrations of naturally radioactive isotopes (and release radon at different rates).
</WorkedExample>

## P7.14 Hazards and applications of ionising radiation

<FormulaCard title="Why ionising radiation is hazardous">
Ionisation can damage DNA within cells, potentially causing malfunction or uncontrolled division (cancer); high doses can destroy cells outright ("radiation sickness"). Danger depends on both radiation type and whether the source is **inside** or **outside** the body.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="Hazard depends on location relative to the body">
**Alpha**: most hazardous *inside* the body (highly ionising, all its energy dumped into nearby cells) but essentially harmless *outside* (can't even get through skin). **Beta**: moderate hazard either way — penetrates skin from outside, still ionising if inhaled/ingested. **Gamma**: hazardous both inside and outside, since it penetrates deep into tissue — though it's the least ionising per unit path length of the three.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Choosing a source for sterilisation, tracing, and thickness gauging">
For each application, what type of radiation (and roughly what half-life) is most appropriate: (a) sterilising plastic syringes; (b) a medical tracer for a procedure lasting a few hours; (c) a thickness gauge for a continuously produced sheet material?

(a) **Gamma** — most penetrating, so it reaches every part of the equipment, and a **long half-life** (years) means the source doesn't need frequent replacing.

(b) **Gamma** — penetrates the body to be detected externally with minimal ionising damage to tissue (alpha or beta would be far too damaging internally); a **short half-life** (hours) limits the patient's radiation exposure once the scan is done, while still lasting long enough to complete the procedure.

(c) **Beta** — alpha would be blocked completely by the sheet (no signal at all), while gamma would pass through almost unaffected by small thickness changes (little sensitivity); beta partially penetrates, with the exact amount sensitive to thickness. A **long half-life** (years) keeps the source's own strength roughly constant, so changes in count rate reflect only thickness changes, not the source running down.
</WorkedExample>

<Tip title="Exposure to radiation doesn't make an object radioactive">
Gamma-sterilised food or equipment isn't left radioactive afterwards — irradiation only ionises atoms/molecules as the radiation passes through; it doesn't turn stable nuclei into unstable ones. This is exactly why gamma sterilisation is considered safe for food and medical equipment.
</Tip>

Standard precautions for anyone working with radioactive sources: store them in lead-lined, clearly labelled containers; keep as much distance as possible (e.g. long-handled tongs); and wear protective clothing — all aimed at minimising exposure, since risk always increases with dose but there's no single "safe threshold" below which harm is guaranteed not to occur.

## P7.15 Interpreting decay graphs

<FormulaCard title="Reading half-life off a graph">
Pick **any** count rate (or percentage of undecayed nuclei) on the graph, then read the time taken for that value to **halve**. Doing this from several different starting points on the same graph should always give the same half-life — that consistency is a useful check that you've read the graph correctly.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Percentage-remaining and count-rate graphs tell the same story">
Since count rate is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei remaining, a graph of "count rate vs time" and a graph of "% undecayed nuclei vs time" for the same source have exactly the same shape and give exactly the same half-life — percentages are just often easier to read precisely since the actual nuclei count can be enormous.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Reading half-life, with an uncorrected background rate">
A graph of measured count rate vs time (not corrected for background) levels off at 20 cpm at large times, and reads 220 cpm at time zero. At $t=50$ min the reading is 120 cpm. Find the half-life.

The steady value the count rate settles towards is the **background rate**, 20 cpm. Source count rate at $t=0$: $220-20=200$ cpm. Source count rate at $t=50$: $120-20=100$ cpm — exactly half of 200. So the half-life is **50 minutes**.
</WorkedExample>

In a sample where a radioactive "parent" nuclide decays into a stable "daughter," the parent's percentage falls exactly as the daughter's percentage rises to match — the two percentages always sum to 100% (assuming none of the daughter nuclei leave the sample).

## P7.16 What half-life means

<FormulaCard title="Half-life">
The **half-life** of a radioactive isotope is the average time taken for half the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay — equivalently, the average time for the sample's count rate to halve.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Half-life doesn't depend on sample size or elapsed time">
However much of the isotope you have, and however long it's already been decaying, the count rate still takes exactly one half-life to halve again from *whatever value it currently is*. Half-life is a fixed property of the **nuclide itself** — the only thing that changes it is which isotope you're dealing with, ranging from tiny fractions of a second to far longer than the age of the universe.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="What does and doesn't affect half-life">
Which of these affects a sample's half-life: (1) the number of unstable atoms present, (2) how long the sample has already been decaying, (3) which radioactive nuclide is present?

Only **(3)** — half-life is a fixed property of the specific nuclide, unaffected by sample size or elapsed decay time.
</WorkedExample>

## P7.17 Half-life calculations

<FormulaCard title="Predicting count rate after n half-lives">
$$
N = N_0\left(\frac12\right)^n
$$

where $N_0$ is the initial count rate (or number/percentage of undecayed nuclei), and $n$ is the number of half-lives elapsed (need not be a whole number, though whole-number cases are the most common in questions).
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Projecting count rate forward using halving steps">
A source has an initial count rate of 4000 cpm and a half-life of 10 h. Find the count rate after 10 h, 20 h, and 50 h.

$$
10\,\text{h} = 1\ t_{1/2}:\ 4000\times\tfrac12 = 2000\ \text{cpm}
$$
$$
20\,\text{h} = 2\ t_{1/2}:\ 4000\times\left(\tfrac12\right)^2 = 1000\ \text{cpm}
$$
$$
50\,\text{h} = 5\ t_{1/2}:\ 4000\times\left(\tfrac12\right)^5 = 125\ \text{cpm}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Finding half-life from two count rates">
A source reads 600 cps initially, and 75 cps after 12 h. Find the half-life.

Count the halvings needed to get from 600 to 75: $600\rightarrow300\rightarrow150\rightarrow75$ — three halvings, so 12 h $=3$ half-lives, giving a half-life of $12\div3=4\ \text{h}$.
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Working both forwards and backwards from the present">
A source has half-life 10 s and a current count rate of 64,000 cps. Find: (a) the count rate 20 s ago; (b) the count rate in 30 s; (c) the time until the count rate reaches 500 cps.

(a) 20 s $=2$ half-lives in the past, so **double** the count rate twice, working backwards: $64\,000\rightarrow128\,000\rightarrow256\,000$ cps.

(b) 30 s $=3$ half-lives ahead, so **halve** three times: $64\,000\rightarrow32\,000\rightarrow16\,000\rightarrow8000$ cps.

(c) Halve repeatedly until reaching 500: $64\,000\rightarrow32\,000\rightarrow16\,000\rightarrow8000\rightarrow4000\rightarrow2000\rightarrow1000\rightarrow500$ — seven halvings, so $7\times10=70\ \text{s}$.
</WorkedExample>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- Nucleus = protons + neutrons (nucleons); electrons orbit outside. Atomic number $Z=$ protons; mass number $A=$ protons + neutrons.
- Proton/neutron mass $\approx1$; electron mass $\approx\frac{1}{2000}$. Proton charge $+1$, electron $-1$, neutron $0$.
- Isotopes: same $Z$, different $A$ (different neutron count). Nuclide notation: ${}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$.
- Ionisation = gain/loss of electrons only; never changes $Z$ or $A$.
- Alpha ($\alpha$, ${}^4_2\text{He}$): most ionising, least penetrating, $Z-2$/$A-4$. Beta ($\beta^-$): intermediate, $Z+1$/$A$ unchanged. Gamma ($\gamma$): least ionising, most penetrating, no change to $Z$ or $A$; uncharged, undeflected by fields.
- Nuclear equations conserve total mass number and total atomic number across the arrow.
- Correct measured count rates for background: source rate = measured rate $-$ background rate.
- Half-life: average time for count rate (or undecayed nuclei) to halve; fixed for a given nuclide, independent of sample size or elapsed time.
- $N=N_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^n$ for $n$ half-lives elapsed; count halvings to find $n$ when working out an unknown half-life.

physics/thermal-physics.title: Thermal Physics
physics/thermal-physics.content:
## P4.1 Thermal energy and conduction

Every substance is made of particles in constant motion — vibrating in place in a solid, moving freely in a liquid or gas. **Thermal energy** is the energy tied up in that motion. It's related to, but not the same thing as, **temperature**: temperature is a measure of how hot something is (roughly, the average speed of its particles), while thermal energy also depends on how much substance you've got.

<Tip title="Heat always flows from hot to cold">
"Heat" is just the name for thermal energy while it's being transferred from one place to another. It always flows from a region at higher temperature to a region at lower temperature — never the other way, unless something else (like a fridge) is doing work to force it.
</Tip>

<FormulaCard title="Conduction">
**Conduction** transfers heat through a substance by particles passing kinetic energy to their immediate neighbours, without the particles themselves travelling anywhere. In a solid, hotter particles vibrate more and jostle the next particles along; in a liquid, it happens through collisions between particles that are also free to drift.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="No particles, no conduction">
Conduction absolutely requires particles to pass energy between — so it **cannot** happen through a vacuum. If a question describes heat crossing empty space (e.g. from the Sun to the Earth), conduction is never the mechanism, however tempting it looks.
</Trap>

## P4.2 Conductors, insulators, and conduction in metals

<FormulaCard title="Good vs poor conductors">
A **good conductor** transfers heat quickly by conduction — metals (solid or molten), especially copper, silver, and gold. A **poor conductor** (an **insulator**) transfers heat slowly — plastics, wood, and gases, including air.
</FormulaCard>

The general trend across states of matter: solids conduct better than liquids, which conduct better than gases — in each step the particles get further apart on average, so collisions (and the energy transfer they carry) become less frequent.

<Tip title="Metals conduct so well because of free electrons">
In a metal, it isn't just the vibrating lattice ions passing energy along slowly, neighbour to neighbour — there's also a sea of **free electrons**, which gain kinetic energy when part of the metal heats up and then carry it rapidly through the whole structure via collisions. Non-metals have no free electrons to do this, which is exactly why they conduct so much more slowly.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Ranking substances by conductivity">
Order liquid water, water vapour, solid aluminium, and ice from best insulator to best conductor.

Aluminium is a metal, so it's easily the best conductor of the four (free electrons). Comparing the remaining three by state: solids conduct better than liquids, which conduct better than gases — so among water in its three forms, ice (solid) beats liquid water, which beats water vapour (gas). Putting it together: water vapour, liquid water, ice, solid aluminium.
</WorkedExample>

Good conductors are used wherever you want heat to pass through quickly — saucepan bases, the plate of an iron. Good insulators are used wherever you want to slow heat down — saucepan and iron handles, blankets, home insulation, and the trapped air layer in double glazing.

## P4.3 Factors affecting rate of conduction

<FormulaCard title="What speeds up conduction">
Rate of conduction is higher for: a **bigger temperature difference** between the two ends, a **better conductor** as the connecting material, a **shorter distance** for heat to travel, and a **larger contact area** between the objects and the connecting material.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="'Contact area' means the whole exposed surface, if the object is fully surrounded">
For heat conducting between two objects joined at a single face, the relevant area is that shared face. But when an object sits inside a surrounding fluid at a different temperature, the relevant contact area is its **entire outer surface** — a larger-surface-area object loses (or gains) heat to its surroundings faster, purely because there's more surface for particle collisions to happen across.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Combining several changes to a double-glazed window">
For each pair of changes below, could the rate of conduction through the window stay unchanged? (1) Thicker glass panes + smaller window area. (2) Air between panes replaced by a better insulating gas + larger window area. (3) Thinner glass panes + air between panes replaced by a vacuum.

(1) Thicker glass (longer conduction distance) *reduces* the rate; a smaller area also *reduces* the rate. Both changes push the same way, so the rate must decrease — **no**, it can't stay unchanged.

(2) A better insulating gas *reduces* the rate, but a larger area *increases* it — these two pull in opposite directions, so it's entirely possible for them to cancel out and leave the rate unchanged — **yes**, this one's plausible.

(3) Thinner glass alone would *increase* the rate — but replacing the gap with a **vacuum** removes conduction between the panes entirely, dropping that part of the rate to zero regardless of anything else. Overall the rate must fall — **no**, it can't stay unchanged.
</WorkedExample>

## P4.4 Density changes with temperature

<FormulaCard title="Heating a fluid lowers its density">
Heating a fluid makes its particles move faster and (if not confined) spread further apart on average — the particles themselves don't get bigger, there's just more empty space between them. Since density is mass per unit volume, spreading the same particles over more volume **lowers the density**.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Why a hot air balloon rises">
Explain why a hot air balloon floats upward when the burner heats the air inside it.

Heating the air inside the balloon lowers its density (same mass of air particles, spread over more volume). Even including the mass of the fabric and basket, the balloon's overall density ends up lower than the density of the cooler air surrounding it — and a less-dense object surrounded by a denser fluid experiences a net upward force, so it rises. Switching off the burner lets the trapped air cool, its density rises back up, and the balloon descends.
</WorkedExample>

## P4.5 Convection currents

<FormulaCard title="Convection, in one line">
Warmer fluid is less dense, so it **rises**; cooler, denser fluid moves in to take its place. Repeated continuously near a heat source, this cycle is a **convection current**.
</FormulaCard>

Notice conduction is actually the *first* step in most convection stories — heat conducts from the source (a radiator, a Bunsen flame) into the fluid immediately touching it. That locally-warmed fluid then rises because it's now less dense, dragging the bulk fluid motion (convection proper) that carries the heat onward far faster than conduction alone ever could.

<Trap title="Heating fluid at the top of a container doesn't set up a convection current">
Convection relies on warmed fluid rising past cooler fluid above it. If the heat source is already at the *top*, the warmed (less dense) fluid has nowhere higher to rise to — it just stays put, and no circulating current develops. This is exactly why an immersion heater or radiator needs to sit low in a room, and a fridge's cooling element needs to sit high, to actually drive circulation.
</Trap>

<FormulaCard title="Conduction vs convection">
Both require particles, and both can happen in fluids — but only **conduction** can happen in a solid (a solid's particles can't flow around in bulk). Conduction passes energy particle-to-particle without the particles relocating; convection moves energy by physically carrying the particles themselves from one place to another.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Where to put the freezer compartment in a fridge">
A fridge has a small freezer compartment with cooling coils inside. Should it go at the top, middle, or bottom of the fridge, and why?

Air cooled by the coils becomes denser and sinks. If the compartment is at the **top**, this cooled air sinks down through the fridge, pushing warmer air (warmed by food or by conduction through the walls) up to the coils to be cooled in turn — setting up a convection current that circulates cold air around the whole interior. Putting the compartment at the bottom would trap the coldest air there with no route to circulate upward, leaving the rest of the fridge poorly cooled.
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="A sea breeze on a sunny day">
On a sunny day, land reaches a higher temperature than the sea. Explain the direction of the breeze at ground level, and why there's a breeze in the opposite direction higher up.

Air above the land is warmed (by conduction from the hot ground) more than air above the sea, so it becomes less dense and **rises**. Cooler air from over the sea flows in along the ground to replace it — so at ground level, the breeze blows **from sea to land**. That rising warm air has to go somewhere once it's up high: it spreads out and flows back **from land to sea** at altitude, completing the convection loop.
</WorkedExample>

Cavity wall insulation exploits this same physics in reverse: an empty cavity between two walls lets convection currents form and actively speed up heat loss, but filling it with foam (full of tiny, separate trapped-air pockets) confines any convection to a scale far too small to matter, leaving only slow conduction through the trapped air.

## P4.6 Thermal (infrared) radiation

<FormulaCard title="Thermal radiation">
Thermal radiation, or **infrared (IR) radiation**, is an electromagnetic wave — it travels at the speed of light and, unlike conduction or convection, needs **no medium** at all. This is how energy reaches the Earth from the Sun across empty space.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Thermal radiation is not ionising radiation">
It's easy to lump "radiation" of every kind together, but infrared is a low-energy part of the electromagnetic spectrum, not a product of unstable nuclei decaying. It isn't ionising, and it doesn't damage cells or DNA the way nuclear radiation can — it's simply electromagnetic waves carrying energy that we sense as warmth.
</Trap>

## P4.7 Absorption and emission

<FormulaCard title="Every object emits and absorbs, all the time">
Any object above absolute zero **emits** thermal radiation — hotter objects emit at a higher rate. Any object that thermal radiation hits either **absorbs**, **reflects**, or **transmits** it; whatever is absorbed increases the object's thermal energy.
</FormulaCard>

Put emission and absorption together and you get the net effect on temperature: an object **hotter** than its surroundings emits faster than it absorbs, so it loses energy net and cools; an object **cooler** than its surroundings absorbs faster than it emits, so it gains energy net and warms — in both cases, tending back towards the surrounding temperature.

<WorkedExample title="Net rate of energy change for a window">
1000 W of thermal radiation hits a window. It reflects 100 W and transmits 750 W, while also emitting 200 W of its own thermal radiation. Find the net rate of change of the window's thermal energy, and say whether it's a gain or a loss.

Of the 1000 W arriving, whatever isn't reflected or transmitted must be **absorbed**: $1000-100-750=150\ \text{W}$ absorbed. The window is also losing energy by emitting its own radiation at 200 W. Net change $=150-200=-50\ \text{W}$ — a **loss** of 50 W.
</WorkedExample>

## P4.8 Factors affecting radiation rates, and applications

<FormulaCard title="Surface texture and area">
For a given temperature, **matt/dull surfaces** absorb and emit thermal radiation at a **higher** rate than **shiny surfaces**, which are poor absorbers and poor emitters (but good reflectors). A **larger surface area** raises both the absorption and emission rate.
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="A good absorber is automatically a good emitter">
This pairing (good absorbers = good emitters; poor absorbers = poor emitters = good reflectors) always holds for the *same* surface, which is exactly why choosing a surface finish involves a trade-off — you can't independently pick "great absorber, terrible emitter."
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Survival blankets and solar water heaters">
Explain why a survival blanket is shiny, and why a solar water heater's pipes are painted matt black.

A survival blanket needs to keep a cold person warm: being **shiny**, it's a poor emitter (so it loses very little of the person's own radiated heat to the surroundings) and a good reflector (so it bounces the person's radiated heat straight back towards them). A solar heater's pipes need to *gain* heat fast: being **matt black**, they're good absorbers of the Sun's incoming radiation — and although a good absorber is also a good emitter, the pipes still heat up net because radiation is arriving from the Sun far faster than the comparatively cool pipes can emit it away.
</WorkedExample>

The same absorption/emission balance, scaled up to the whole planet, explains the greenhouse effect: if the Earth and its atmosphere absorb thermal radiation faster than they emit it back out to space, there's a net gain of thermal energy and the planet warms.

## P4.9 Heat capacity and specific heat capacity

<Tip title="Net heat transfer is what decides temperature change">
An object can be gaining heat by one process and losing it by another at the same time — what matters for its temperature is the **net** transfer. More heat in than out, and it warms up (particles speed up on average); more heat out than in, and it cools (unless it happens to be changing state, in which case temperature can stay fixed despite the energy transfer — that's covered separately under changes of state).
</Tip>

<FormulaCard title="Specific heat capacity">
$$
c = \frac{\text{thermal energy}}{\text{mass}\times\text{temperature change}}
$$

Specific heat capacity $c$ (units $\text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$) is the energy needed to raise **1 kg** of a substance by **1 °C**. It's a property of the *substance* — heat capacity (without "specific"), by contrast, is a property of one particular object and already factors in its mass.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Heat capacity and specific heat capacity are not interchangeable">
Heat capacity (units $\text{J}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$) describes a specific object of fixed mass; specific heat capacity (units $\text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$) describes the substance itself, independent of how much of it you have. Two blocks of the same metal but different sizes share the same specific heat capacity but have different heat capacities.
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Calculating specific heat capacity from an experiment">
A 3.0 kg sample of an unknown metal rises in temperature by 15 °C when 45 000 J of thermal energy is transferred to it. Find its specific heat capacity.

$$
c = \frac{\text{thermal energy}}{\text{mass}\times\text{temperature change}} = \frac{45\,000}{3.0\times15} = 1000\ \text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}
$$
</WorkedExample>

<WorkedExample title="Finding energy transferred from a temperature drop">
A 2.0 kg aluminium block ($c=900\ \text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$) cools from 25.0 °C to 20.0 °C. Find the energy transferred to the surroundings.

Temperature change: $25.0-20.0=5.0\ {}^\circ\text{C}$.

$$
\text{thermal energy} = c\times\text{mass}\times\text{temperature change} = 900\times2.0\times5.0 = 9000\ \text{J}
$$
</WorkedExample>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- Thermal energy relates to particle motion; heat always flows from hot to cold. Conduction needs particles — impossible through a vacuum.
- Metals conduct well because free electrons carry energy fast; solids > liquids > gases in general.
- Conduction rate ↑ with bigger temperature difference, better conductor, shorter distance, larger contact area.
- Heating a fluid lowers its density (particles spread out); less-dense fluid rises, denser fluid sinks — this drives convection currents.
- Convection needs a fluid (not solids); heating from the top prevents a current forming.
- Thermal (infrared) radiation is electromagnetic — travels at light speed, no medium needed, not ionising.
- Hotter objects emit radiation faster; net absorption/emission decides whether an object warms or cools relative to its surroundings.
- Matt/dark surfaces: good absorbers and emitters. Shiny surfaces: poor absorbers and emitters, good reflectors.
- $c=\dfrac{\text{thermal energy}}{\text{mass}\times\text{temperature change}}$, units $\text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$ — a property of the substance, not a specific object.

physics/waves.title: Waves
physics/waves.content:
## P6.1 Wave properties, wave equation

A wave is a pattern of vibrations (oscillations) that transfers **energy** from a source to whatever absorbs it — with **no net transfer of matter** in that direction. When you speak, no air travels from your mouth to a listener's ear; only the vibration pattern does. Ripples on a pond move water up and down, but they don't carry water outwards.

<Trap title="Something can move up and down without matter being transferred">
A boat bobbing as an ocean wave passes doesn't mean the wave is carrying water (or the boat) along with it — the water just oscillates about a fixed average position. Don't confuse local oscillation with a genuine flow of matter in the direction of travel.
</Trap>

Waves come in two geometric flavours, based on how the vibration direction relates to the direction of travel:

<FormulaCard title="Transverse vs. longitudinal">
- **Transverse**: vibration is **perpendicular** to the direction of energy transfer. Examples: all electromagnetic waves, waves on a string, seismic S-waves.
- **Longitudinal**: vibration is **parallel** to the direction of energy transfer. Examples: sound, ultrasound, seismic P-waves, compressions on a slinky.

Water waves are a mixture of both — particles move in ellipses — but still have no net motion in the direction of travel.
</FormulaCard>

A transverse wave's pattern is described by **peaks** and **troughs**; a longitudinal wave's by **compressions** (particles pushed together, locally higher pressure) and **rarefactions** (particles pulled apart, locally lower pressure).

<FormulaCard title="Defining amplitude, wavelength, period, frequency">
- **Wavelength** ($\lambda$) — distance between adjacent peaks/troughs (or adjacent compressions/rarefactions).
- **Amplitude** — maximum displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position.
- **Period** ($T$) — time for one complete oscillation (seconds).
- **Frequency** ($f$) — oscillations per unit time (Hz); $1\ \text{Hz} = 1$ oscillation per second.

$$
f = \frac{1}{T}
$$
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Reading amplitude, frequency, wavelength off a physical setup">
A vibrator produces ripples that travel at $1.2\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$; a floating cork bobs 20 times per minute, moving 8.0 mm from the top to the bottom of its motion. Find the period, frequency, wavelength and amplitude.

$$
T = \frac{60}{20} = 3.0\ \text{s}, \qquad f = \frac{1}{T} = 0.33\ \text{Hz}
$$

Wavelength = distance travelled by the wave in one period: $\lambda = 1.2 \times 3.0 = 3.6\ \text{cm}$.

Amplitude is *half* the peak-to-trough distance (since amplitude is measured from equilibrium): $\dfrac{8.0}{2}=4.0\ \text{mm}$.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Amplitude is peak-to-equilibrium, not peak-to-trough">
The vertical distance you read off a diagram between a peak and the next trough is *twice* the amplitude — halve it before reporting a value.
</Trap>

<FormulaCard title="Wave speed and the wave equation">
$$
\text{wave speed} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}, \qquad v = f\lambda
$$

Wave speed is the speed of an identifiable feature of the wave (a peak, a compression) moving through the medium.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Two swimmers and a passing wave">
Two swimmers 12 m apart (along the wave's direction of travel) each bob up and down with period 5.0 s; when one is at a peak the other is at the next trough. Find the wavelength, frequency and speed.

Peak-to-trough is half a wavelength, so $\lambda = 2\times12=24\ \text{m}$.

$f = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{1}{5.0}=0.20\ \text{Hz}$.

$v = f\lambda = 0.20\times24=4.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (matches distance/time: the peak takes half a period, 2.5 s, to cross the 12 m gap, giving $12/2.5=4.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ directly).
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Unit prefixes for short times and high frequencies">
$1\ \text{ms}=10^{-3}\ \text{s}$, $1\ \mu\text{s}=10^{-6}\ \text{s}$, $1\ \text{ns}=10^{-9}\ \text{s}$; $1\ \text{kHz}=10^3\ \text{Hz}$, $1\ \text{MHz}=10^6\ \text{Hz}$, $1\ \text{GHz}=10^9\ \text{Hz}$.
</Shortcut>

**Ranging** (finding distance from wave speed and travel time) always uses the same idea — a pulse travels *there and back*, so halve the round-trip distance:

<FormulaCard title="Ranging with reflected pulses">
$$
\text{distance to object} = \frac{1}{2}\times\text{wave speed}\times\text{time for pulse to return}
$$

Used for laser range-finding, radar, sonar, and ultrasound scanning.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Ultrasound A-scan of the eye">
Ultrasound travels at $1550\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ inside the eye. Reflections return at $t_0=4.0\ \mu\text{s}$ (front of eye), $t_3=8.0\ \mu\text{s}$ (front of lens), $t_2=13.0\ \mu\text{s}$ (back of lens), $t_1=40.0\ \mu\text{s}$ (back of eye). Find the length of the eye and the thickness of the lens.

$$
\text{length of eye} = \tfrac{1}{2}v(t_1-t_0) = \tfrac12(1550)(36\times10^{-6}) = 0.028\ \text{m} = 2.8\ \text{cm}
$$

$$
\text{lens thickness} = \tfrac{1}{2}v(t_2-t_3) = \tfrac12(1550)(5.0\times10^{-6}) = 0.0039\ \text{m} = 3.9\ \text{mm}
$$
</WorkedExample>

Mechanical waves (sound, seismic waves, water waves) need a material medium — no particles, no wave. **Electromagnetic waves** (radio through gamma) are vibrations of electric and magnetic fields, need no medium, and travel through a vacuum at the speed of light.

<Trap title=""In space no one can hear you scream" — but they could see you">
Sound is a mechanical, longitudinal wave, so it needs particles to vibrate and cannot cross a vacuum — a scream in space is silent. Light, however, is electromagnetic and *can* cross a vacuum, so you'd still be visible. Don't mix up which property (mechanical vs. electromagnetic) is doing the work in each statement.
</Trap>

## P6.2 Reflection, refraction, and the Doppler effect

<FormulaCard title="Law of reflection">
$$
i = r
$$

The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal, with both rays and the normal in the same plane. This holds at every point on a surface — a smooth surface has parallel normals everywhere (orderly reflection, forms images); a rough surface has randomly oriented normals (diffuse, scattered reflection).
</FormulaCard>

Reflection keeps the wave in the *same medium*, so its **speed, frequency, and wavelength are all unchanged** — only direction changes.

Refraction happens when a wave crosses a boundary into a medium where it travels at a different speed (and isn't travelling along the normal).

<FormulaCard title="Direction of refraction">
- Wave **slows down** → refracts **towards** the normal (e.g. air → glass).
- Wave **speeds up** → refracts **away from** the normal (e.g. glass → air).
- Wave travelling along the normal ($i=0$) → no change in direction, but speed still changes.
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="What changes and what doesn't">
| | Frequency | Wavelength | Direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reflection | unchanged | unchanged | changes (law of reflection) |
| Refraction, speed increases | unchanged | increases | away from normal |
| Refraction, speed decreases | unchanged | decreases | towards normal |

Frequency never changes at a boundary — every crest that arrives must leave, so the rate is preserved. Wavelength then follows from $v=f\lambda$: since $f$ is fixed, $\lambda$ scales with $v$.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Reasoning about frequency, wavelength and speed together">
Light reflects off a silvered-back mirror, refracting into the glass, reflecting, then refracting back out. Compare wavelength and speed at points in air (A, D) versus inside the glass (B, C).

Frequency is unchanged throughout (reflection and refraction both preserve it). Speed is lower in glass, so B and C share one (lower) speed while A and D share another (higher) speed. Wavelength tracks speed via $v=f\lambda$ with $f$ fixed, so wavelength is shorter at B, C than at A, D — and since A and D are both in air, they share the same wavelength as each other.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="Energy at a boundary splits three ways">
At any boundary, incident energy is shared between **reflected**, **refracted (transmitted)**, and **absorbed** energy — total reflection or total transmission are special cases, not the default. Energy is conserved across the three.
</Trap>

Water waves in a ripple tank behave analogously to light in a ray box (same laws of reflection/refraction), but the analogy has limits: light is electromagnetic and can cross a vacuum; water waves are mechanical and cannot.

<FormulaCard title="The Doppler effect">
Relative motion between source and observer shifts the received wavelength and frequency:

| Relative motion | Wavelength | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| At rest relative to each other | unchanged | unchanged |
| Approaching | shorter | higher |
| Receding | longer | lower |

Only motion **along the line joining source and observer** matters — purely perpendicular motion (e.g. a source circling the observer at constant distance) produces no Doppler shift.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Circling at constant radius gives zero Doppler shift">
If a buzzing insect flies in a circle around your head, the distance between you never changes, so despite the motion there's no shift — you hear the true emitted frequency throughout, not something in between "approaching" and "receding."
</Trap>

<WorkedExample title="Cosmological redshift">
Distant galaxies' spectral lines are observed at longer wavelengths than the same lines measured from stationary lab sources, with the shift larger for more distant galaxies. What does this imply about galactic motion?

An increased wavelength is a "receding" Doppler shift, so distant galaxies are moving away from us. A larger shift means a larger recession speed, so more distant galaxies are receding faster than nearer ones.
</WorkedExample>

Doppler shifts of reflected waves (radar "speed guns," ultrasound blood-flow monitors) let you measure the speed of whatever reflected the pulse, since the shift size scales with relative speed.

## P6.3 Optics: ray diagrams for reflection and refraction

<FormulaCard title="Ray-diagram vocabulary">
- **Ray** — direction of energy transfer.
- **Normal** — line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence.
- **Angle of incidence ($i$)** / **angle of reflection ($r$)** / **angle of refraction** — all measured from the normal, not the surface.
</FormulaCard>

For a **plane mirror**, the image of a point source forms behind the mirror at the same perpendicular distance as the source is in front — because every reflected ray obeys $i=r$ and the rays appear to diverge from that single point behind the glass. Curved mirrors obey the same law, but the normal at each point is perpendicular to the *tangent* to the curve there, not to some fixed plane.

<WorkedExample title="Rotating a mirror doubles the ray's turn">
A mirror is turned through $2°$ about the point where a ray strikes it. By how much does the reflected ray turn?

The normal rotates with the mirror, by $2°$. The incident ray direction is fixed, so the incident angle also changes by $2°$; since $r=i$ always, the reflected angle changes by the same $2°$. The reflected ray's own direction shifts by the *sum* of the incident- and reflected-angle changes: $2°+2°=4°$.
</WorkedExample>

<Shortcut title="Rule of thumb: mirror rotation doubles the ray deflection">
Whenever a mirror rotates by angle $\theta$ about the point of incidence (with the incident ray fixed), the reflected ray deflects by $2\theta$ — useful for optics questions on rotating mirrors and galvanometers alike.
</Shortcut>

For **refraction**, the same slows-down/speeds-up rule from P6.2 applies ray by ray. A rectangular block (parallel faces) refracts the ray back parallel to its original direction, since the two boundaries produce equal and opposite bends; a triangular prism does not restore the original direction, since the faces aren't parallel — and since different wavelengths of light travel at (slightly) different speeds in glass, white light spreads into a spectrum, with blue deviating more than red.

<WorkedExample title="Apparent depth: why a pool looks shallower than it is">
Light leaves a pebble at the bottom of a pool and refracts into air at the surface. Explain why the pool looks shallower than it actually is.

Light travels faster in air than in water, so rays refract *away from* the normal on leaving the water, diverging more than before. Tracing the diverging rays backwards, they appear to originate from a point *above* the pebble's true position — so the pebble (and the pool floor) looks shallower than it really is.
</WorkedExample>

<Trap title="A ray along the normal never bends — check this case first">
If an incident ray happens to lie along the normal, it passes straight through every boundary undeviated, even though its speed still changes. Many "which diagram is correct" questions hinge on spotting this special case being violated (a ray shown bending despite arriving along the normal, or shown straight despite arriving at an angle).
</Trap>

## P6.4 Sound waves

Sound is produced by a **vibrating source** — a loudspeaker cone, a string, an air column, vocal cords — which sets the surrounding medium vibrating in the same pattern.

<FormulaCard title="Source vibration vs. sound produced">
- Sound frequency = source vibration frequency.
- Sound amplitude depends on source vibration amplitude.
- Sound **speed** is set by the **medium**, not the source.
</FormulaCard>

Sound is **longitudinal**: particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel, forming alternating compressions and rarefactions, and — needing particles to vibrate — sound cannot cross a vacuum (the classic bell-in-a-jar demonstration: the bell stays visible as air is pumped out, but becomes inaudible).

<FormulaCard title="Loudness and pitch">
- **Loudness** $\leftrightarrow$ amplitude — bigger amplitude, louder sound.
- **Pitch** $\leftrightarrow$ frequency — higher frequency, higher pitch.

On an oscilloscope trace (voltage against time, not a literal picture of the longitudinal wave): taller peaks = louder; closer-together peaks = shorter period = higher pitch.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="An oscilloscope trace of sound looks transverse but isn't">
The wiggly line on an oscilloscope screen represents *voltage against time* from a microphone, not the physical motion of air particles. Sound itself is longitudinal even though its oscilloscope trace looks like a transverse wave — don't infer the wave type from the shape of the display.
</Trap>

Sound obeys the law of reflection, producing **echoes** — heard later than the direct sound because the reflected path is longer, even though direct and reflected waves travel at the same speed.

<FormulaCard title="Distance from an echo/pulse round trip">
$$
d = \frac{vt}{2}
$$

$t$ is the round-trip time; halve it because the pulse travels there *and* back. Used for sonar, echolocation, and ultrasound scanning.
</FormulaCard>

<WorkedExample title="Timing hand-claps to match an echo">
A man stands 170 m from a cliff. At what frequency should he bang wood blocks together so each echo arrives exactly halfway between hits? (Speed of sound = 340 m/s.)

Round-trip distance $=2\times170=340\ \text{m}$, so echo delay $=340/340=1.0\ \text{s}$. For the echo to land halfway between hits, the gap between hits must be double the echo delay: $2.0\ \text{s}$, so $f=1/T=1/2.0=0.50\ \text{Hz}$.
</WorkedExample>

<FormulaCard title="Range of human hearing">
$20\ \text{Hz}$ to $20\ \text{kHz}$. Using $\lambda = v/f$ with $v_{\text{sound in air}}=330\ \text{m s}^{-1}$: audible wavelengths run from $16.5\ \text{m}$ (at 20 Hz) down to $1.65\ \text{cm}$ (at 20 kHz) — low frequency corresponds to long wavelength, and vice versa.
</FormulaCard>

**Ultrasound** is just sound above 20 kHz: same longitudinal-wave physics, same need for a medium, just too high-pitched for most humans to hear. It's used for sonar (locating objects/measuring depth underwater), medical scanning (each tissue boundary partially reflects a pulse, and timing the returns builds an image), and crack detection in solids — all using the same $d=vt/2$ round-trip logic.

<WorkedExample title="Sonar depth-finding">
A boat's sonar pulse returns after 0.40 s; ultrasound travels at $1500\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in water. Find the depth.

$$
d = \frac{vt}{2} = \frac{1500\times0.40}{2} = 300\ \text{m}
$$
</WorkedExample>

## P6.5 The electromagnetic spectrum

<FormulaCard title="Properties shared by all EM waves">
- All are **transverse**.
- All need **no medium** and can cross a vacuum.
- All travel at the **speed of light**, $c=3.00\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, in a vacuum — but slower in other media.
- They consist of vibrating **electric and magnetic fields**, not vibrating particles — this is *why* they can cross a vacuum.
</FormulaCard>

Any accelerating/vibrating charge emits EM waves; every object above absolute zero contains vibrating charged particles and therefore emits a spectrum of EM radiation, with hotter objects emitting more radiation and shifted towards higher frequencies (a cool stone emits only infra-red; metal heated hot enough glows red, then white).

<FormulaCard title="The seven regions, in order of increasing frequency / decreasing wavelength">
Radio → Microwave → Infra-red → Visible → Ultraviolet → X-ray → Gamma-ray

Regions overlap at their boundaries (a wave can be validly labelled either of two neighbouring names); X-rays and gamma-rays of the same wavelength are physically identical and are usually distinguished only by *how* they were produced (electrons hitting a target vs. radioactive decay).
</FormulaCard>

<FormulaCard title="Frequency-wavelength relationship for EM waves">
$$
c = f\lambda \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad f=\frac{c}{\lambda}, \qquad \lambda=\frac{c}{f}
$$

Since $c$ is fixed (in a vacuum), frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional: long-wavelength radio waves have the lowest frequencies, short-wavelength gamma-rays have the highest.
</FormulaCard>

<Trap title="Crossing a medium boundary changes speed and wavelength, never frequency">
Exactly as with any other wave (P6.2), an EM wave's frequency is fixed by its source and stays constant as it crosses into a new medium. Speed changes because of the medium, and wavelength changes to match via $v=f\lambda$ — frequency is the one quantity that never moves.
</Trap>

<FormulaCard title="Applications and hazards, by region">
| Region | Typical application | Typical hazard |
|---|---|---|
| Radio | broadcasting, radio astronomy | low, unless extremely intense |
| Microwave | satellite/mobile/Wi-Fi comms, cooking | tissue heating, cataracts |
| Infra-red | heaters, remote controls, thermal imaging | skin burns |
| Visible | sight, telescopes, lasers | retinal damage from intense sources |
| Ultraviolet | fluorescence, sterilisation | sunburn, skin cancer, retinal damage |
| X-ray | medical imaging, security scanning | ionising — cell/DNA damage, cancer |
| Gamma-ray | radiotherapy, sterilisation, tracers | ionising — cell damage, mutation |
</FormulaCard>

<Tip title="Ionisation is the dividing line for the most serious hazards">
High-frequency, short-wavelength EM waves (X-ray, gamma-ray, some UV) carry enough energy per photon to **ionise** atoms in tissue, directly damaging molecules (including DNA). Lower-frequency, longer-wavelength waves can't ionise, but can still cause **heating** — which is why microwave and infra-red hazards are about burns rather than mutation.
</Tip>

<WorkedExample title="Stretching the early universe's radiation">
As the universe expands, EM wavelengths are stretched. Which conversions are physically possible: gamma-rays → microwaves, or X-rays → infra-red?

Both are possible, since in each pair the second-named radiation has the longer wavelength. (This is genuinely how the cosmic microwave background formed — early-universe gamma radiation stretched into today's microwaves.) A conversion the *other* way, towards shorter wavelength, would not be possible from stretching alone.
</WorkedExample>

## Formula and shortcut summary

- $f=\dfrac{1}{T}$; $v=f\lambda$; wave speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}$. Amplitude is measured from equilibrium — halve a peak-to-trough reading.
- Transverse: vibration $\perp$ travel direction (all EM waves, string waves). Longitudinal: vibration $\parallel$ travel direction (sound, ultrasound).
- Mechanical waves need a medium; EM waves don't, and travel at $c=3.00\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in a vacuum.
- Reflection: $i=r$; speed, frequency, wavelength all unchanged. Refraction: frequency unchanged, wavelength and direction follow the speed change (slow down → bend towards normal & shorter $\lambda$; speed up → bend away & longer $\lambda$). A ray along the normal never bends.
- Doppler effect: only relative motion *along the source–observer line* matters. Approaching → shorter $\lambda$, higher $f$. Receding → longer $\lambda$, lower $f$. Perpendicular motion → no shift.
- Round-trip ranging (echoes, sonar, radar, ultrasound): $d=\dfrac{vt}{2}$.
- Human hearing: 20 Hz–20 kHz, i.e. 16.5 m down to 1.65 cm in air. Ultrasound is just sound above 20 kHz.
- EM spectrum order (increasing $f$, decreasing $\lambda$): radio, microwave, infra-red, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma-ray. $c=f\lambda$, frequency constant across any boundary.
